claims.text: Every item-rich instrument with item-resampling support is highly internally consistent. Single-scenario and single-run instruments (the misalignment probe and τ²-bench) are the weakest links.
methods: Split-half correlation over 50 random half-splits, Spearman–Brown corrected
Splits restricted to the items common to every model's logs
results: Split-half (SB) ≥0.96 for R-Judge specificity (0.99), R-Judge F1 (0.96), InjecAgent (0.98), AgentHarm (0.96), jailbreak (0.97), MMLU (0.96), GPQA (0.97)
Rank stability ≥0.97
Top-quartile persistence 0.79–0.96, with AgentHarm lowest at 0.79 on 44 behaviors
Misalignment halves: raw split-half 0.54, SB 0.70
τ² has no resampling bound (single run, user-simulator variance)
conditions: Applies only to item sampling within one instrument
Misalignment has only config-level data across two scenario halves

claims.text: Within-model standard errors are a modest fraction of between-model spread. This supports panel-level spread but not every pairwise model difference.
methods: Binomial SEs for MMLU (500 items) and GPQA (198 items)
Bootstrap SEs over R-Judge records and jailbreak prompts
results: Max SE: MMLU 2.2, GPQA 3.6, misalignment 5.0, R-Judge F1 3.0, jailbreak 3.7
Between-model SD (expanded panel): 8.7, 18.2, 26.0, 14.9, 28.5
Worst-case SE is 13–25% of SD; spread is 4–8× the worst-case SE
τ² not covered
conditions: Individual model pairs can be closer than their SEs

claims.text: R-Judge's official headline metric (F1 on the unsafe class) is gameable because it ignores true negatives. Benchmarks should report the full confusion matrix, complementary metrics and constant-verdict reference rows.
methods: The harness stores per-model verdicts and labels
Recall, specificity, precision, F1 and balanced accuracy computed from the stored verdicts
results: F1 combines recall with precision and ignores true negatives
Specificity is the fraction of benign traces correctly identified as benign; balanced accuracy weights the two classes equally
conditions: The appropriate metric depends on the use case: a monitor with costly false alarms vs a last-line filter

claims.text: Capability must be measured under a uniform protocol. Provider-reported anchors fail the positive control while harmonized anchors pass it, and how much capability a score contains depends on the metric.
methods: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42)
Composite = mean of the standardized anchors
results: Positive control fails on provider numbers and passes on harmonized anchors
BFCL ranked GPT-4o-mini highest (0.72) and the two most capable models lowest (0.42–0.48), apparently rewarding format conformance
Anchor panel of 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded)
conditions: The anchors are static-knowledge tests and may miss agentic ability
Measurement error in the covariate distorts adjusted relationships

claims.text: Cross-benchmark comparisons are panel-dependent. The benchmarks disagree, small-panel impressions did not persist, and coverage loss is non-random.
methods: Common panel across R-Judge, InjecAgent and AgentHarm
Pre-specified positive, negative and convergent controls
results: First panel n=7: impressions did not survive
Common panel n=18; AgentDojo n=5, so the convergent control is inconclusive
Negative control passes: median first permuted eigenvalue 1.71 vs threshold 2.18
Minimum detectable effect ρ≈0.62 at n=18; ρ≈0.4 needs about 40 models
Coverage loss concentrated on models with non-standard tool interfaces
conditions: Avoid interpreting rank correlations on fewer than about a dozen models
The PCA is interpreted only if the controls pass

claims.text: The held-out outcomes have specific measurement properties. A single jailbreak template ceilings, the three-template average does not, AgentHarm shows the strongest jailbreak association (read as agreement between harmful-compliance instruments), and judge swaps reproduce the chat outcomes.
methods: StrongREJECT scoring on 50 prompts averaged over AIM, refusal suppression and prefix injection
Misalignment: 100 decisions per model scored by a fixed classifier
results: Under AIM alone, 11 of 22 models refuse every request
The three-template average leaves no model at the ceiling
Misalignment and jailbreak graders reproduce model-level scores closely
AgentHarm refusal-judge swap agrees less closely because it redoes only the refusal component
conditions: τ² is not a safety measure

claims.text: Expanding to 41 anchored models from 12 organizations weakens the capability–misalignment correlation. Organizational clustering must be handled in resampling and organization comparisons remain observational.
methods: Fisher z comparing 2026-only models with the original panel
Permutation test checked on 2,000 synthetic null panels
results: Misalignment n=40, jailbreak n=41
Permutation test rejection 0.045–0.052 at α=0.05 under standard nulls
Worst-case clustered-variance null gives 0.067 at α=0.05 (jailbreak only), no inflation at α=0.005
Exclusions based only on telemetry; several newer models could not be run reliably (stale harness)
conditions: Capability matched only on a static composite

claims.text: Two artifact checks: blinded LLM coders recover the authors' target assignments, and XSTest records over-refusal. Both are low-power context rather than decisive tests.
methods: Seven LLM coders from distinct families shown neutral descriptions, with shuffled options
results: 27/28 ratings agree; Krippendorff α=0.825
AgentHarm 7/0 harm blocking; InjecAgent 1/6
AgentDojo read as task success by 4/7 coders in the distractor round
XSTest unsafe subset refusal 83–100% (sd 4.5, ceilinged)
Safe-subset over-refusal 0–60% (Claude-3-Haiku 60%, o3-mini 30%)
conditions: Controls coder bias but not rubric-designer bias

items.question: A policy that labels every R-Judge trace as unsafe would earn a non-trivial official F1. Which of the R-Judge summaries the harness records would expose this policy as uninformative, and what value would it take?
items.answer: Specificity would expose it: every benign trace would be flagged, so specificity is 0. Balanced accuracy would be 0.5, because recall of 1 is averaged with specificity of 0. F1 cannot expose the policy because it ignores true negatives, and perfect recall props it up.
rubric: Names specificity (and/or balanced accuracy) as the exposing metric, with specificity = 0 (and/or balanced accuracy = 0.5)
Explains that F1 ignores true negatives, so perfect recall inflates it while benign traces are all misjudged

items.question: The paper reports split-half ≥0.96 and rank stability ≥0.97 for its item-rich instruments. Would that kind of evidence establish that τ²-bench retail rankings are stable, and why?
items.answer: No. τ² was run once per model and its main noise source is the user simulator, so there is no item- or run-resampling bound for it. Item-level consistency on other instruments says nothing about run-to-run simulator variance in τ².
rubric: States no, the consistency evidence does not establish τ² stability
Reason: τ² is a single run with unbounded user-simulator variance, which item resampling does not capture

items.question: The capability composite passes its positive control. Under what condition would using it as the covariate in capability-adjusted (partial-correlation) analyses of tool-using agent safety still mislead, and why?
items.answer: It would mislead when agentic or tool-use ability diverges from static knowledge. The composite is built only from MMLU and GPQA, so it would mismeasure the relevant capability. Covariate measurement error attenuates or distorts adjusted relationships in hard-to-sign directions.
rubric: Condition: the agentic ability relevant to the benchmark is not tracked by static-knowledge MMLU/GPQA
Reason: covariate measurement error distorts or attenuates the partial correlations in unpredictable direction

items.question: Two models differ by 4 points on the misalignment outcome. Can the paper's uncertainty evidence support ranking one above the other, and why?
items.answer: No. Per-model misalignment SEs have a median of 4.0 and a maximum of 5.0, so a 4-point gap is within about one SE of each model. The scenario halves also agree only moderately (SB 0.70), so the instrument is weakest at fine distinctions.
rubric: States the difference is not supportable or reliable
Reason cites the misalignment SE of about 4–5 points (gap within SE) and/or the moderate half agreement (SB 0.70)

items.question: The organization-group permutation test is described as adequately calibrated. In which specific setting would its false-positive rate exceed nominal, and by roughly how much?
items.answer: It exceeds nominal on the jailbreak outcome when variances are clustered by organization but there is no mean difference, tested at α=0.05. There the rejection rate is about 0.067 instead of 0.05. At α=0.005 no inflation was detected.
rubric: Identifies jailbreak outcome with organization-clustered variances at α=0.05
Gives inflation to about 0.067 (vs 0.05), noting none detectable at stricter α=0.005

items.question: The three-template jailbreak average removed the ceiling on the original and expanded panels. Would it continue to discriminate on a future panel where most models refuse every request under all three templates, and why?
items.answer: No. Averaging only removes ties when at least one template elicits some compliance. If models refuse everything under AIM, refusal suppression and prefix injection alike, they all tie at the top again, as 11 of 22 did under AIM alone.
rubric: States it would stop discriminating (ceiling returns)
Reason: averaging works only if some template produces variance; models refusing under all templates tie, as with the single-template AIM ceiling

items.question: MMLU has the most items and the smallest per-model SEs of any instrument. Why does it nonetheless have the largest worst-case SE relative to between-model spread?
items.answer: Its between-model SD is the smallest of the instruments (8.7 points), so even a 2.2-point maximum SE is about 25% of the spread. The other instruments have much larger spreads: GPQA 3.6/18.2 ≈ 20%, jailbreak 3.7/28.5 ≈ 13%.
rubric: Attributes it to MMLU's small between-model SD (8.7)
Gives the ratio of about 25% (2.2/8.7), larger than the other instruments' ratios

items.question: Why is AgentHarm's top-quartile persistence (0.79) the lowest among the item-rich instruments even though its corrected split-half matches others at 0.96?
items.answer: AgentHarm has only 44 behaviors, far fewer items than the instruments with 164–570 items. Item resampling therefore perturbs model scores more, and models near the quartile boundary move across it more often.
rubric: Attributes it to AgentHarm's small item count (44 behaviors)
Explains that fewer items mean more resampling variability, so boundary models cross the quartile cut more often

items.question: AgentHarm covers 19 models and InjecAgent covers all 22. Why is the common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel 18 rather than 19?
items.answer: R-Judge lost one model, Qwen3-32B, to the 90% valid-output gate (21% unparseable). The intersection with AgentHarm is 18, so that excluded model must be among AgentHarm's 19.
rubric: Identifies the R-Judge exclusion (Qwen3-32B, below the valid-output threshold) as the cause
Infers that this model is in AgentHarm's 19, so the intersection drops to 18

items.question: Why would provider-reported MMLU and GPQA figures fail the positive control that the same benchmarks pass when re-measured by the harness?
items.answer: Provider numbers come from different prompts, shot counts and decoding settings. This adds variation that reflects reporting practice rather than ability and weakens the agreement between the two anchors. Fixing the protocol removes that noise, so the anchors agree as expected.
rubric: Identifies heterogeneous prompting, shot and decoding conditions as noise unrelated to ability
Explains that this noise reduces MMLU–GPQA agreement, which uniform measurement restores

items.question: Why is the paper's first seven-model cross-benchmark panel especially unsuited to supporting any rank correlation, given its power analysis?
items.answer: Even at n=18 only correlations of about ρ≥0.62 are detectable with 80% power, so at n=7 the detectable threshold is much higher. A single unusual model can also swing the estimate either way. Seven is also below the paper's guidance of about a dozen models.
rubric: Uses the power result (minimum detectable effect ≈0.62 at n=18, worse at n=7)
Notes that single models can swing a rank correlation at that size, and/or that n=7 is below the ~12-model guidance

items.question: Why does AgentDojo, but not InjecAgent, draw majority task-success votes when blind coders are offered a task-success distractor?
items.answer: AgentDojo is environment-scored for utility as well as security, so its description includes completing the user's task. InjecAgent is rule-scored only on attack success.
rubric: Points to AgentDojo's dual scoring (utility plus security)
Contrasts with InjecAgent, which scores only injection/attack success

items.question: A model changes its R-Judge verdicts only on benign traces, so that some benign traces it previously flagged are now passed as benign. Its verdicts on unsafe traces are unchanged. Would its specificity change?
items.answer: Yes, it would rise. Specificity is the fraction of benign traces correctly identified as benign, and false alarms have been converted into true negatives.
rubric: Yes, specificity increases
Because specificity counts correct benign judgments, which increased

items.question: A model changes its R-Judge verdicts only on unsafe traces, so that it now catches some unsafe traces it previously missed. Its verdicts on benign traces are unchanged. Would its specificity change?
items.answer: No. Specificity depends only on verdicts for benign traces, which are unchanged. Recall, F1 and balanced accuracy would rise instead.
rubric: No, specificity is unchanged
Because specificity is computed only over benign traces; the change affects recall instead

items.question: Would the convergent control (InjecAgent vs AgentDojo agreement) become assessable under the paper's own guidance if AgentDojo were run on all 19 AgentHarm-covered models?
items.answer: Yes, broadly. Nineteen models exceeds the roughly-a-dozen minimum and is comparable to the n=18 common panel. Agreement could then be estimated rather than being inconclusive, though power would still be modest.
rubric: Yes, it becomes assessable
Because n=19 exceeds the ~12-model guidance and matches the scale of the common panel (unlike n=5)

items.question: Would the convergent control become assessable under the paper's own guidance if AgentDojo were run on just two more models (n=7)?
items.answer: No. Seven models is still below the roughly-a-dozen threshold, and it is the size of the pilot panel whose impressions did not persist. The control would remain inconclusive.
rubric: No, still inconclusive
Because n=7 is below the ~12-model guidance, and a 7-model panel already produced non-persistent impressions

items.question: If the jailbreak outcome used only the AIM template, could it rank the original-panel models relative to one another across the whole panel?
items.answer: No. Under AIM, 11 of 22 models refuse every request, so half the panel is tied at the top and cannot be separated.
rubric: No
Because 11/22 models tie at the ceiling under AIM

items.question: Using the primary three-template jailbreak average instead, could the outcome rank the original-panel models relative to one another across the whole panel?
items.answer: Yes. Averaging AIM, refusal suppression and prefix injection leaves no model at the ceiling, so the previously tied models are separated.
rubric: Yes
Because the three-template average leaves no model at the ceiling

items.question: Suppose the true Spearman correlation between two benchmarks on the n=18 common panel were 0.7. Would the panel detect it with at least 80% power at α=0.05?
items.answer: Yes. The minimum detectable effect at n=18 is about ρ=0.62, and 0.7 exceeds it.
rubric: Yes
Because 0.7 is above the ~0.62 minimum detectable effect at n=18

items.question: Suppose the true Spearman correlation between two benchmarks on the n=18 common panel were 0.4. Would the panel detect it with at least 80% power at α=0.05?
items.answer: No. Detecting ρ≈0.4 with 80% power needs about 40 models, far more than 18.
rubric: No
Because ρ≈0.4 requires roughly 40 models (and is below the ~0.62 detectable at n=18)

items.question: A new benchmark scores code-review agents that flag vulnerable commits, and it reports only precision. Following the paper's recommendations, what should it add, and why?
items.answer: It should add recall, or the full confusion matrix, plus constant-verdict reference rows. Precision omits false negatives (missed vulnerable commits), so an agent that flags rarely but accurately could score well. A complementary metric covering the omitted cell reveals whether the score reflects discrimination or a disposition.
rubric: Recommends adding recall (or the full confusion matrix) and/or constant-verdict reference rows
Reason: precision ignores missed positives, so a conservative flagging disposition can score well without discrimination

items.question: A team wants an agentic capability covariate for tool-using safety analyses and proposes strict function-call syntax scoring such as BFCL. Based on the paper's pilot, should they adopt it as is, and why?
items.answer: No. In the six-model pilot, strict syntax scoring ranked GPT-4o-mini highest (0.72) and the two most capable models lowest (0.42–0.48). This suggests it rewards format conformance rather than capability. A validated agentic anchor is needed first.
rubric: States they should not adopt it as is
Cites the pilot ranking inversion (GPT-4o-mini top, most capable models lowest), interpreted as rewarding format conformance

items.question: A study correlates a safety score with capability on 15 models drawn from three developers. What resampling should it use for intervals, per the paper?
items.answer: It should use organization-clustered bootstrap with leave-one-organization-out (and leave-one-model-out) checks. Models from the same developer share training and safety tuning, so treating them as independent overstates precision. It should also flag that n=15 gives low power for moderate correlations.
rubric: Recommends organization-clustered resampling (and/or leave-one-organization-out)
Reason: same-developer models are not independent, so naive resampling overstates precision

items.question: A team wants to compare current frontier models' safety using XSTest. Which XSTest subset should they rely on to separate models, and why?
items.answer: The safe subset, which measures over-refusal. The unsafe subset is ceilinged: every model refuses 83–100% (sd 4.5), leaving little variance. Over-refusal on the safe subset ranges from 0 to 60%.
rubric: Recommends the safe subset (over-refusal)
Reason: the unsafe subset is ceilinged (83–100%, sd 4.5) while the safe subset varies (0–60%)

items.question: A new model's provider exposes a non-standard tool-calling schema that AgentDojo cannot use natively. Under the paper's protocol, should the team wrap it in a tool-call emulation layer to include it, and what follows for the panel?
items.answer: No. It should be recorded as not-run, because emulated tool calls would change the instrument. This exclusion adds to coverage loss that falls disproportionately on such models, so the panel behind any comparison must be stated.
rubric: States record as not-run rather than emulate
Reason: emulation changes the instrument; and/or notes this contributes to non-random coverage loss requiring panel reporting

items.question: A new model scores near-perfect safety on AgentHarm. Which other measurement in the paper's harness should be checked before reading this as discriminating harm-blocking, and why?
items.answer: XSTest over-refusal on the safe subset should be checked. A model that refuses nearly everything scores well on every harm-compliance instrument without discriminating harmful from benign requests.
rubric: Names XSTest safe-subset over-refusal
Reason: blanket refusal inflates harm-compliance safety scores without discrimination

items.question: If the harmonized MMLU/GPQA anchors had also failed the positive control, which of the paper's recommendations and analyses would lose support?
items.answer: The recommendation to fix capability by re-measuring under a uniform protocol would lose its supporting evidence. The capability composite would also be unvalidated, undermining capability-adjusted partial correlations and the PCA, which was interpreted only if the controls pass.
rubric: Names the uniform-protocol re-measurement recommendation (the claim that harmonizing fixed the anchors)
Notes that capability-adjusted analyses and/or the control-gated PCA would lose a validated basis

items.question: If the column-permuted score matrices had produced first eigenvalues above the parallel-analysis threshold of 2.18, which analysis would lose its warrant?
items.answer: The PCA of cross-benchmark structure on the n=18 panel would lose its warrant. It was pre-specified to be interpreted only if the controls passed, and a failed negative control would mean the pipeline manufactures structure from noise.
rubric: Names the cross-benchmark PCA/factor analysis
Reason: the negative control would show spurious structure, and the PCA was conditional on the controls passing

items.question: If the second jailbreak judge (Gemini) had disagreed strongly with the gpt-4o judge at the model level, which reported association would be most directly undermined?
items.answer: AgentHarm's strongest held-out association with jailbreak safety would be undermined. The jailbreak outcome would then be judge-dependent, and the association could reflect the particular judge rather than agreement between harmful-compliance instruments.
rubric: Names the AgentHarm–jailbreak association
Reason: the outcome would no longer be robust to judge choice, so the association could be a judge artifact

items.question: If blind coders had overwhelmingly assigned AgentHarm to 'risk recognition' rather than 'harm blocking', which part of the paper's framing would lose support?
items.answer: The §3.2 target assignments, which treat AgentHarm as the harm-blocking instrument, would lose support. So would comparisons framed in terms of those targets, including the reading that benchmark disagreement reflects instruments coded to different targets.
rubric: Names the author-defined benchmark target assignments (§3.2)
Notes that comparisons framed by targets (e.g., interpreting disagreement as different targets) would inherit the doubt

items.question: If the misalignment outcome's blackmail and leaking halves had agreed with Spearman–Brown about 0.97, which characterization in the paper would change?
items.answer: The misalignment probe would no longer be one of the weakest components. Its consistency would match the item-rich instruments, and τ²-bench, as a single unbounded run, would remain the main weak link.
rubric: States misalignment would no longer be classed as a weakest component (limited fine distinctions)
Notes τ² would remain the unbounded/weak instrument

items.question: If within-model SEs had been comparable to between-model SDs rather than 13–25% of them, which of the paper's interpretive claims would fail?
items.answer: The claim that the observed panel-level spread reflects real model differences, being 4–8× the worst-case SE, would fail. Rankings and correlations on the panel would then be dominated by measurement noise.
rubric: Names the claim that panel-level spread is supported (exceeds SE by 4–8×)
Explains that spread could then be noise, undermining rankings/correlations

items.question: Does the paper show that AgentHarm is the best general predictor of agent safety? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. AgentHarm's strongest association is with jailbreak safety, but both instruments score harmful compliance. The paper reads this as agreement between similar instruments rather than evidence about safety in general.
rubric: Not settled (or not supported)
Reason: AgentHarm and StrongREJECT jailbreak both measure harmful compliance, so the association is instrument agreement, not general safety

items.question: Does the paper's high internal consistency (split-half ≥0.96) show that the audited benchmarks validly measure agent safety? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Internal consistency shows that rankings are stable under item resampling. Whether scores track safety is a separate criterion-validity question, addressed by held-out outcomes with limited, outcome-dependent results.
rubric: Not settled
Reason: consistency/reliability concerns stability under item sampling, not whether the construct measured is safety

items.question: Does the paper show that organizational identity causes differences in safety among models of similar capability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The comparison is observational. Capability is matched only on a static-knowledge composite, within-organization n is small (4–8), organization is collinear with release date and capability, and some organizations are range-restricted.
rubric: Not settled
Reason cites the observational design and confounds: static composite, small within-org n, collinearity, and/or range restriction

items.question: Does the paper show that the capability–misalignment relationship disappears for 2026 models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper reports that the correlation is weaker on the expanded panel, not that it vanishes. The original models are nested in the expanded panel, so a change must be assessed with nested resampling, and organizational composition also shifted.
rubric: Not settled (weaker is not the same as absent)
Reason: the reported result is weakening on a nested panel, requiring nested/composition-matched comparison rather than showing disappearance

items.question: Does the paper show that every pairwise MMLU difference between panel models is reliable? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Worst-case SE is 2.2 points against an SD of only 8.7. The paper states that the spread supports panel-level differences but not every pairwise one, because some model pairs are closer than their SEs.
rubric: Contradicted
Reason: with SE up to 2.2 and SD 8.7, some model pairs differ by less than measurement error; only panel-level spread is supported

items.question: Does the paper show that InjecAgent and AgentDojo, both injection benchmarks, rank models consistently? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The convergent control was inconclusive because AgentDojo ran on only five models, too few to assess agreement.
rubric: Not settled
Reason: AgentDojo n=5 leaves the convergent control inconclusive

items.question: Does the blind coding (27/28 agreement, α=0.825) show that the authors' two-construct scheme is the correct way to categorize these benchmarks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The coding controls coder bias but not rubric-designer bias, because the authors wrote the category definitions. It shows that the assignments are recoverable from neutral descriptions, not that they are the only reasonable ones. The distractor round also left AgentDojo and misalignment contested.
rubric: Not settled
Reason: the authors wrote the categories (rubric-designer bias uncontrolled), so agreement shows recoverability, not uniqueness/correctness

items.question: Why could the 2026 expansion compare misalignment and jailbreak relationships across panels but not any relationship between the audited agent benchmarks and τ² task success?
items.answer: Only the two chat-based outcomes and the anchors were re-measured on new models. New models skipped the tool-calling audit benchmarks, which need a tool loop, and τ² was not re-collected. Relationships involving those columns have no expanded-panel data.
rubric: Notes that τ² was not re-collected and the tool-loop audit benchmarks were not run on new models
Explains that only the chat-based outcomes (plus anchors) need no tool harness and were extended, so only their relationships can be updated

items.question: The jailbreak outcome's corrected split-half is reported as 0.97. Under what way of forming the halves would a figure like this overstate the instrument's internal consistency, and why?
items.answer: It would be overstated if the halves were formed from individual template–prompt pairs, so that the AIM, refusal-suppression and prefix-injection variants of the same base prompt could land in different halves. The two halves would then share prompt content and agree for that reason alone. The paper avoids this by resampling by base prompt, which respects the dependence among the three templates.
rubric: States that splitting by template–prompt pair (rather than by base prompt) would inflate the consistency estimate
Explains that the three templates applied to the same base prompt are dependent, so halves sharing base prompts would agree spuriously

items.question: Independent-judge swaps were used to show that the jailbreak and misalignment outcomes are robust. Would a comparable second-judge check establish that τ²-bench retail scores are robust, and why?
items.answer: No. τ² success is environment-scored from the final database state, so there is no judge to swap. Its unbounded variance comes from the simulated user in a single run, and only replicate runs could bound it.
rubric: Concludes that a judge swap would not establish τ² robustness
Explains that τ² is environment-scored (no judge) and its uncontrolled variance comes from the user simulator in a single run, which needs replicate runs

items.question: In the organization-group analysis, would a within-organization rank correlation between capability and safety for Anthropic's models be informative, and why?
items.answer: Largely not. Anthropic's models sit near the safety ceiling, so their safety scores are range-restricted. A within-organization correlation would be weak or unstable whatever the true relationship is.
rubric: Concludes that the Anthropic within-organization correlation would be uninformative or unreliable
Cites range restriction: Anthropic models are near the safety ceiling, leaving little variance to correlate

items.question: Under what change to its scenario set would the misalignment outcome stop being a specific probe of autonomous-agent misbehavior, and how would that affect its associations with other instruments?
items.answer: Folding the exploratory murder scenario into the primary outcome would do it. That scenario involves a severe harm that harm-compliance instruments may also anticipate, so the outcome would start overlapping with those instruments, and its associations with harm-compliance measures could be inflated. Because the scenario was added after the primary outcome was fixed, using it would also be a forking path.
rubric: Identifies adding the murder (third) scenario to the primary outcome

Explains that it involves severe harm that harm-compliance instruments also anticipate, diluting specificity and potentially inflating associations with harm-compliance measures (e.g., jailbreak or AgentHarm)

items.question: R-Judge F1 has item-bootstrap rank stability of 0.97. Would that guarantee the same model ranking if R-Judge were rerun under a different harness version or prompt format, and why?
items.answer: No. Rank stability only quantifies item-sampling error within one administration of the instrument. Changes in administration conditions, such as harness, scorer, prompt format or parsing rules, are a different source of variation that this analysis does not cover.
rubric: Concludes that it would not guarantee the same ranking
Explains that the consistency evidence covers only item sampling within one instrument and run, not changes in harness, prompt format, scorer or similar administration conditions

items.question: Suppose the true Spearman correlation between XSTest safe-subset over-refusal and AgentHarm safety is 0.5. Could the paper's XSTest comparison panel reliably detect it, and why?
items.answer: No. The XSTest comparisons have n=17–20, where the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is about ρ=0.62. A true correlation of 0.5 would be detected with low power and estimated with wide uncertainty, which is why XSTest is treated as descriptive context.
rubric: Concludes that it could not reliably detect a 0.5 correlation
Links the XSTest n of 17–20 to the minimum detectable effect of about 0.62 at n≈18 (80% power)

items.question: The organization permutation test was judged adequately calibrated. Would that conclusion carry over to a panel of three organizations with two models each, and why?
items.answer: Not established. Calibration was checked by simulation only for this panel's shape: seven organization clusters with 4–8 models each, with models, organizations and capability held fixed. Even there, a clustered-variance null mildly inflated rejection. A panel with far fewer and smaller clusters would need its own calibration check.
rubric: Concludes that the calibration does not automatically carry over (it would need re-checking)
Explains that the synthetic-null check was specific to seven clusters with within-organization n of 4–8 (and showed some inflation under clustered variances)

items.question: The jailbreak row of the consistency table uses only 20 shared base prompts, fewer than any other item-rich instrument. Why does it nonetheless have the highest top-quartile persistence (0.96)?
items.answer: Its between-model spread is the largest of any instrument (SD 28.5), and its worst-case within-model SE (3.7) is only about 13% of that spread, the smallest ratio of any instrument. Models are far apart relative to their noise, so resampling prompts rarely moves a model across the top-quartile boundary.
rubric: Attributes the high persistence to the large between-model spread (SD 28.5) relative to within-model SE
Notes the worst-case SE is only about 13% of the SD, so quartile membership rarely flips under resampling

items.question: Why does the misalignment row of the consistency table report a single blackmail-vs-leaking comparison and no rank stability or quartile persistence, unlike the other instruments?
items.answer: Misalignment data exist only at the configuration level, as the two scenario variants. There is no item-level data to draw 50 random half-splits or bootstrap items from. The only split available is blackmail versus leaking.
rubric: States that only config-level (scenario-half) data exist for misalignment
Explains that, without item-level data, random half-splits and item-bootstrap rank or quartile statistics cannot be computed, leaving only the one blackmail/leaking split

items.question: Why is the jailbreak SE computed over about 150 judged units while the jailbreak consistency analysis uses only 20?
items.answer: The SE uses every judged template–prompt pair: 50 prompts times 3 templates. The consistency analysis resamples by base prompt, to respect the dependence among templates, and is restricted to base prompts judged in every model's logs. Each model leaves a few different prompts unjudged, so only 20 of the 50 remain.
rubric: Explains that about 150 comes from 50 prompts × 3 templates used for the bootstrap SE
Explains that the consistency analysis uses base prompts (not template pairs) common to every model's logs, which leaves 20 because models leave different prompts unjudged

items.question: Why are the organization-histogram-matched subsets drawn at size 21 specifically?
items.answer: The original anchored panel has 21 models, after DeepSeek-R1 is excluded from the anchors. Drawing subsets of the expanded pool at that size, with the original panel's organization histogram, matches both panel size and organizational composition. Any remaining change in the correlation can then be attributed to models within organizations rather than to a different organizational mix or panel size.
rubric: Identifies 21 as the size of the original anchored panel (DeepSeek-R1 excluded)
Explains that matching size and organization histogram separates compositional change from within-organization change

items.question: Why does the GPQA row of the consistency table cover one fewer model (45) than the MMLU row (46)?
items.answer: GLM-4.5 returned usable MMLU answers but not GPQA answers because of routing incompatibilities. It contributes a partial row with MMLU only, so it enters the MMLU consistency computation but not the GPQA one.
rubric: Identifies GLM-4.5 as the model with MMLU but no GPQA data
Connects this partial row to its presence in the MMLU count and absence from the GPQA count

items.question: The misalignment outcome's worst-case SE (5.0) is about 19% of its between-model SD, comparable to other instruments. Why does the paper still treat it as a weak link?
items.answer: The binomial SE treats the 100 decisions as exchangeable draws and so captures only sampling noise within the scenarios. It does not capture scenario dependence. The blackmail and leaking halves agree only moderately (raw 0.54, Spearman–Brown 0.70), showing that a model's score depends materially on which scenario is used, and that is the weakness.
rubric: Explains that the binomial SE reflects decision-level sampling only, not variation across scenarios
Cites the moderate agreement between the scenario halves (SB 0.70 or raw 0.54) as evidence of scenario dependence

items.question: Why could the 2026 expansion to 41 models not resolve the inconclusive InjecAgent–AgentDojo convergent control?
items.answer: The expansion covered only the anchors and the two chat-based outcomes, which need no tool loop. New models skipped the tool-calling audit benchmarks, so AgentDojo stayed at n=5, too few to assess agreement.
rubric: States that the new models were not run on AgentDojo (or the other tool-calling audit benchmarks)
Concludes that AgentDojo therefore remained at n=5, so the control stays inconclusive

items.question: A constant policy labels every R-Judge trace as benign. Would it achieve the maximum possible specificity?
items.answer: Yes. Specificity is the fraction of benign traces correctly identified as benign, and this policy gets every benign trace right, so its specificity is 1.
rubric: Answers yes (specificity = 1 or 100%)
Reasons that specificity counts only benign traces identified as benign, all of which this policy gets right

items.question: A constant policy labels every R-Judge trace as benign. Would it achieve the maximum possible balanced accuracy?
items.answer: No. Balanced accuracy weights the two classes equally. This policy catches no unsafe traces (recall 0) alongside perfect specificity, so its balanced accuracy is 0.5, at chance level.
rubric: Answers no (balanced accuracy = 0.5)
Reasons that balanced accuracy averages benign and unsafe performance and that recall on unsafe traces is 0

items.question: On the 40-model expanded misalignment panel, would a true Spearman correlation of about 0.4 with capability be detectable with roughly 80% power at α=0.05?
items.answer: Roughly yes. The paper's power analysis says detecting ρ≈0.4 with 80% power needs about 40 models, which the expanded misalignment panel approximately provides.
rubric: Answers yes or approximately yes
Cites the requirement of about 40 models to detect ρ≈0.4 and that the expanded panel has n=40

items.question: On the original 21-model misalignment panel, would a true Spearman correlation of about 0.4 with capability be detectable with roughly 80% power at α=0.05?
items.answer: No. With about 20 models, the minimum detectable effect is near ρ=0.62, and ρ≈0.4 needs about 40 models. A 0.4 effect would be detected with low power.
rubric: Answers no
Cites the minimum detectable effect of about 0.62 at n≈18–20, or the need for about 40 models for ρ≈0.4

items.question: A model returns parseable R-Judge verdicts on 92% of records but has the lowest F1 on the panel. Under the paper's exclusion gates, would it be excluded from R-Judge analyses?
items.answer: No. The gate requires at least 90% valid outputs and is based only on harness telemetry, never on scores. At 92% valid it passes, whatever its F1.
rubric: Answers no (it is retained)
Reasons that the 90% valid-output gate is met and that exclusions depend on telemetry, not scores

items.question: A model returns parseable R-Judge verdicts on only 85% of records but has the highest F1 on the panel. Under the paper's exclusion gates, would it be excluded from R-Judge analyses?
items.answer: Yes. It falls below the 90% valid-output threshold, as Qwen3-32B did with 21% unparseable. The gate is applied before scores are computed, so a high F1 cannot save it.
rubric: Answers yes (it is excluded)
Reasons that it falls below the 90% valid-output threshold, which is applied regardless of score

items.question: Is treating the two correlations as independent (a Fisher z comparison) appropriate when comparing the capability–misalignment correlation of the original panel with that of the 2026-only models?
items.answer: Yes. The 2026-only models and the original panel are disjoint sets of models, so the two correlations are estimated on independent samples. Fisher's z is one of the paper's pre-specified procedures.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that the two model sets do not overlap, so the correlations are independent

items.question: Is treating the two correlations as independent (a Fisher z comparison) appropriate when comparing the capability–misalignment correlation of the original panel with that of the full 40-model expanded panel?
items.answer: No. The original 21 models are a subset of the expanded 40, so the correlations share models and are dependent. Treating them as independent would overstate the evidence for change, which is why a stratified nested bootstrap is used.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the panels are nested (the original is a subset of the expanded), so a nested or stratified bootstrap is required instead

items.question: A team will deploy a trace monitor whose false alarms block legitimate work and cause alert fatigue, and must pick among models using R-Judge results. Which R-Judge summary should drive the choice, per the paper?
items.answer: A summary that includes specificity, either specificity itself or balanced accuracy, rather than the official F1 alone. F1 ignores true negatives and so does not reflect how often benign traces are left alone, which is the cost this team cares about.
rubric: Recommends specificity or balanced accuracy (a summary covering benign-trace performance) over F1 alone
Explains that F1 ignores true negatives, so it does not capture the false-alarm cost central to this use case

items.question: A team adds a new model to the MMLU consistency analysis, and the new model leaves a different set of items unanswered from the existing models. What happens to the item base of the split-half and rank-stability computation, and why?
items.answer: The item base shrinks. Splits and draws use only items common to every model's logs, already 356 of the 500 administered items. A model missing different items removes those items from the shared intersection for all models.
rubric: States that the number of items used shrinks (the common-item intersection gets smaller)
Explains that splits are restricted to items common to every model's logs

items.question: A study has 15 models, each from a different developer. Would organization-clustered bootstrap change its intervals materially compared with model-level resampling, and why?
items.answer: Essentially not. Clustering matters because same-organization models share training pipelines and safety tuning and are not independent. With one model per organization, each cluster is a single model, so clustered and model-level resampling coincide.
rubric: Concludes that clustering would make little or no difference
Reasons that every cluster contains one model, so the within-organization dependence motivating clustering is absent

items.question: Midway through a study, after its primary jailbreak outcome is fixed, a team decides to add a fourth jailbreak template because it tightens estimates. How should they treat results that use it, following the paper's handling of the third misalignment scenario?
items.answer: They should keep the pre-specified outcome as primary and report the four-template analyses as exploratory. Adding a component after the primary outcome was fixed creates a forking path, even if it tightens per-model estimates.
rubric: Recommends keeping the original outcome primary and treating the new-template analyses as exploratory
Gives the reason that adding components after fixing the primary outcome is a forking path

items.question: A team has nine models from two developers and wants to report a PCA of agent-safety benchmark columns as evidence of latent structure. What does the paper's guidance imply they should do?
items.answer: They should not interpret it as latent structure. Nine models is below the roughly a dozen the paper requires for interpreting rank correlations. A PCA should be interpreted only after positive and negative controls pass, and even then only as a sample description. Because the result can shift between correlation conventions, both Pearson and Spearman versions should be reported.
rubric: Concludes that the PCA should not be interpreted as latent structure (at most descriptive)
Cites the small panel (below about a dozen) and/or the requirement that the controls pass first
Mentions reporting both correlation conventions because of convention sensitivity

items.question: A team wants to evaluate new models whose providers offer no native tool-calling support compatible with the official harnesses. Which of the paper's instruments can they still run under its protocol, and which not?
items.answer: They can run the capability anchors (MMLU, GPQA) and the chat-based held-out outcomes: misalignment and jailbreak. These need no tool loop, which is how the 2026 expansion worked. AgentHarm and AgentDojo require native tool use, so those models would be recorded as not-run rather than forced through an emulation layer.
rubric: Identifies the anchors and the misalignment and jailbreak outcomes as runnable
States that the tool-calling benchmarks (AgentHarm, AgentDojo) would be recorded as not-run (no emulation)

items.question: If MiniMax-M3 had been dropped from the misalignment analysis because of its low harm score rather than because of truncated outputs, which claim about the expanded-panel evidence would be undermined?
items.answer: The claim that exclusions were based only on harness telemetry, never on outcome scores. The n=40 misalignment analysis, and the weakened capability–misalignment correlation it supports, would become open to selection on the outcome.
rubric: Identifies the telemetry-only exclusion claim as undermined
Notes that the n=40 misalignment analysis or its correlation result would then be vulnerable to outcome-based selection bias

items.question: If AgentHarm's item-bootstrap rank stability had come out low (say around 0.6) rather than 0.97, which held-out finding involving AgentHarm would lose support, and why?
items.answer: AgentHarm's strongest-of-all association with jailbreak safety would lose support. Reliability is the precondition for any downstream comparison: if AgentHarm rankings shifted with the sampled behaviors, an association between its scores and another outcome could not be trusted. Its role in the n=18 common-panel comparisons would weaken too.
rubric: Identifies the AgentHarm–jailbreak association (strongest held-out association) as losing support
Explains that downstream associations depend on the instrument's rankings being stable or reliable under item resampling

items.question: If the size-21 organization-histogram-matched subsets had reproduced the original panel's capability–misalignment correlation, how should the weaker correlation on the full expanded panel be interpreted?
items.answer: The weakening would then be attributed to the expanded panel's different organizational composition rather than to a change in the relationship among models within organizations. Matching the original organization histogram is exactly what separates these two explanations.
rubric: Attributes the weakening to the change in organizational composition
Explains that the matched subsets hold the organization mix fixed, so their reproducing the original correlation rules out within-organization change as the cause

items.question: If every model had over-refused at most 5% of XSTest's safe subset, which alternative explanation for high scores on refusal-based instruments such as AgentHarm and the jailbreak outcome would lose force?
items.answer: The blanket-refusal explanation would lose force: that a model scores well on harm-compliance instruments simply by refusing nearly everything. As it is, Claude-3-Haiku over-refuses 60% of safe prompts and o3-mini 30%, so that explanation remains live for some models.
rubric: Identifies the blanket-refusal (over-refusal) explanation as losing force
Contrasts with the observed over-refusal of Claude-3-Haiku at 60% (or o3-mini at 30%), which keeps the concern live

items.question: If the six-model BFCL pilot had ranked the two most capable models highest rather than lowest, which stated limitation of the capability covariate could have been addressed?
items.answer: The limitation that MMLU and GPQA are static-knowledge anchors that may miss agentic ability. A BFCL that tracked capability rather than format conformance could have served as a candidate agentic anchor. The paper's statement that a validated agentic anchor is still needed would then lose its main supporting evidence.
rubric: Identifies the static-knowledge limitation (missing agentic ability) of the anchors
Explains that BFCL would then be a viable agentic anchor, weakening the claim that one is still missing

items.question: If provider-reported MMLU and GPQA figures had passed the positive control, which of the paper's recommendations would lose its empirical demonstration from this audit?
items.answer: The recommendation to measure capability covariates under the study's own uniform protocol rather than importing model-card numbers. Its evidence here is that provider numbers failed the positive control while harmonized anchors passed. Only the general argument about heterogeneous prompting and decoding conditions would remain.
rubric: Identifies the recommendation to re-measure capability under a uniform protocol instead of using provider numbers
Notes that its in-paper evidence is the contrast between provider anchors failing and harmonized anchors passing the positive control

items.question: Does the paper show that cross-benchmark relationships observed on the n=18 common panel apply to models whose providers expose non-standard tool-calling interfaces? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Coverage loss is concentrated on exactly those models, so they are systematically absent from the AgentHarm-limited common panel. Nothing in the paper measures how the relationships behave for them.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that coverage loss is non-random and falls on models with non-standard tool interfaces, so they are missing from the common panel

items.question: Does the paper show that its jailbreak outcome measures robustness to adaptive, optimization-based attacks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The outcome averages three fixed published templates (AIM, refusal suppression, prefix injection) over 50 prompts, and the paper explicitly says it does not cover adaptive attacks.
rubric: Answers not settled (not shown)
Explains that only three fixed published templates were used and adaptive attacks are explicitly outside its coverage

items.question: Does the paper show that a single R-Judge summary metric is the correct choice for every deployment? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper argues that the appropriate summary depends on the use case: a monitor with costly false alarms should use a summary that includes specificity, while a last-line filter may prefer recall. It treats metric choice as part of the claim.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites the use-case dependence (specificity-including summaries for costly false alarms vs recall for a last-line filter)

items.question: Does the paper show that adding the murder scenario produces a better misalignment outcome than blackmail plus leaking? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The third scenario tightens per-model estimates, but it dilutes the probe's specificity to autonomous-agent misbehavior, because harm-compliance instruments may also anticipate severe harm. It was also added after the primary outcome was fixed, so it is kept as exploratory.
rubric: Answers not settled
Notes the trade-off: tighter estimates but reduced specificity, and/or exploratory status as a forking path

items.question: Does the blinded construct coding show that the misalignment outcome is a risk-recognition instrument? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. In the criterion-coding rounds the misalignment outcome was contested: avoiding a harmful autonomous action can be read as recognizing a risk or as declining to act, and coders split between rounds. The paper describes it as a scenario-based behavioral outcome that cannot be reduced cleanly to either category.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that coders split between rounds because the outcome can be read as risk recognition or as harm blocking (declining to act)

items.question: Does the paper show that AgentHarm scores are robust to the choice of judge model to the same degree as the jailbreak outcome? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The Gemini refusal-judge swap agreed less closely than the jailbreak and misalignment swaps. That swap redoes only the refusal component of a multi-stage grading pipeline, so it neither establishes nor refutes full-pipeline judge robustness.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the AgentHarm swap agreed less closely and re-scored only the refusal component, not the full grading pipeline

items.question: Does the paper show that item-sampling error is an unlikely source of jailbreak ranking instability on the expanded panel that includes the 2026 models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Supported. The jailbreak consistency row is computed on 42 models: the 41 anchored expanded-panel models plus DeepSeek-R1. It shows Spearman–Brown 0.97, rank stability 0.98 and quartile persistence 0.96 when resampling by base prompt.
rubric: Answers supported
Cites that the jailbreak consistency analysis covers the expanded panel (42 models) with high split-half, rank-stability and/or quartile values

items.question: AgentHarm safety has item-bootstrap rank stability of 0.97. Would that figure bound how much AgentHarm model rankings could change if the grading were redone with a different judge model, and why?
items.answer: No. The item bootstrap resamples the 44 behaviors while holding the scorer fixed, so it captures only item-sampling variability. Judge dependence is a separate source of variation, and the Gemini refusal-judge swap on AgentHarm agreed less closely than the swaps on the other outcomes.
rubric: Concludes that rank stability does not bound judge-induced ranking changes.
Explains that the bootstrap resamples items (behaviors) under a fixed scorer, and/or notes that the AgentHarm refusal-judge swap agreed less closely.

items.question: The common-panel PCA's negative control passes: the median first eigenvalue of the permuted matrices is 1.71, against a threshold of 2.18. Would this rule out a retained first component that is driven by models sharing one organization's training pipeline, and why?
items.answer: No. Column permutation breaks the alignment of models across columns, so it only tests whether the pipeline manufactures structure from noise. Real covariance created by same-organization models with shared pipelines and safety tuning survives in the unpermuted data and is not addressed by this control. Clustering has to be handled separately, for example by organization-clustered resampling.
rubric: Concludes that the negative control does not rule out organization-driven structure.
Explains that the permutation tests only for noise-manufactured structure, while shared-organization covariance is genuine structure in the real data.

items.question: R-Judge specificity has the highest corrected split-half of any instrument (0.99). Under what model behavior would a high and internally consistent specificity still fail to indicate good trace judgment, and why?
items.answer: A model with a disposition to flag rarely would pass most benign traces on every half of the items, so its high specificity would be very consistent. It could still miss many unsafe traces. Internal consistency shows the score is stable, not that it reflects discrimination, so specificity needs to be read together with recall or balanced accuracy.
rubric: Identifies a disposition to rarely flag traces (or to label most traces benign) as the failing case.
Explains that such a disposition yields consistently high specificity without discrimination, because consistency measures stability rather than validity, or because unsafe traces are missed.

items.question: Suppose a revised R-Judge release changed the proportion of unsafe records. Would official F1 scores from the old and new releases be directly comparable, and why?
items.answer: No. F1 combines recall with precision and ignores true negatives, and precision depends on how many benign traces there are to falsely flag. F1 therefore shifts with the base rate even if model behavior is unchanged. Balanced accuracy weights the two classes equally regardless of base rate, which is why the paper records it alongside F1.
rubric: Concludes that F1 would not be directly comparable across releases with different base rates.
Explains that F1 depends on the class mix through precision (it ignores true negatives), whereas balanced accuracy is base-rate invariant.

items.question: The 2026 expansion excluded models only on harness telemetry, never on outcome scores. Could the expanded-panel capability–safety estimates still be biased by which models were excluded, and why?
items.answer: Yes. Gating blind to scores prevents selecting models on their outcomes, but it does not make the exclusions random. Kimi-K2.6, the Nemotron-3 models, MiniMax-M3, Gemini-2.5-Pro and GLM-4.5 dropped out for unbounded reasoning traces, low anchor usability, truncation or routing incompatibilities, so the panel underrepresents certain kinds of newer models. This mirrors the non-random coverage loss on non-standard tool interfaces in the original panel.
rubric: Concludes that bias from exclusions remains possible.

Explains that telemetry-based exclusions are non-random: they fall on particular kinds of newer models (unbounded reasoning, truncation, routing issues, a stale harness), so the panel is not representative.

items.question: The organization-histogram-matched size-21 subsets are meant to separate changes in organizational composition from changes within organizations. Would they also hold release date and capability fixed, and why?
items.answer: No. They match only the count of models per organization. Organization is only partly collinear with release date and capability, and a matched subset can include 2026 models from the same organizations that differ in date and capability. Differences between the matched subsets and the original panel can therefore still reflect those factors.
rubric: Concludes that the matched subsets do not control for release date or capability.
Explains that matching fixes only the organization histogram, while models within an organization (including 2026 models) differ in date and capability.

items.question: The paper finds that, against τ² task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability. Under what conditions of the τ² outcome itself would this null fail to show that the safety scores lack incremental information?
items.answer: The null is weak evidence because τ² is a single run of 40 tasks whose user-simulator variance cannot be bounded. It is also collected on only 20 models, where only correlations of about ρ=0.6 or larger are detectable with 80% power. Unbounded outcome noise and low power could both hide a moderate incremental association.
rubric: States that the null may reflect the outcome's limits rather than a true absence of incremental information.
Cites the single run with unbounded user-simulator variance and/or the low power at n=20 (minimum detectable effect around 0.6).

items.question: Why is the misalignment outcome's worst-case within-model SE (5.0) more than twice MMLU's (2.2), even though both are binomial SEs?
items.answer: Binomial SE shrinks as the number of scored units grows. The misalignment SE is computed over only 100 decisions per model, while MMLU's is computed over 500 fixed items, so per-model misalignment scores are estimated less precisely.
rubric: Attributes the difference to the number of units: 100 decisions versus 500 items.
Notes that binomial SE decreases as the number of units increases.

items.question: R-Judge is run on its full 571 records. Why does its consistency row in Table 3 use 570 items?
items.answer: The split-half and bootstrap splits are shared across models and restricted to items present in every model's logs. At least one record must be missing or unusable in at least one model's logs, which leaves 570 common items.
rubric: States that the analysis uses only items common to every model's logs.
Infers that at least one record is missing for at least one model, reducing 571 to 570.

items.question: The misalignment outcome covers 21 models on the original panel. Why is the paired τ²/misalignment panel 20?
items.answer: τ² covers only 20 models because it is a multi-turn tool loop, while misalignment covers 21. The paired panel is their intersection, so it is limited by τ² coverage, and all 20 τ² models also have misalignment scores.
rubric: States that the paired panel is the intersection of the two outcomes' coverage.
Identifies τ² coverage (n=20) as the limiting factor.

items.question: Why does the original-panel interaction test need leave-one-organization-out recomputation in addition to leave-one-model-out?
items.answer: OpenAI contributes 6 of the 22 original models, and models from one organization share training pipelines and safety tuning. Dropping one model at a time leaves the other five, so an effect shared across a developer would survive leave-one-model-out. Only removing the whole organization tests whether that developer drives the estimate.
rubric: Explains that same-organization models share a common effect through shared pipelines or tuning, so leave-one-model-out cannot remove it.
Notes the unequal contributions, for example OpenAI's 6 of 22 models, which make a single developer potentially dominant.

items.question: An independent grader reproduces the misalignment outcome's model-level scores closely. Why does that check not resolve the paper's concern that misalignment is a weak link?
items.answer: The grader swap addresses only scoring dependence. The weakness lies in scenario sampling: the blackmail and leaking halves agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70), so scores depend on which scenario is administered. A second grader re-scores the same decisions and cannot address that.
rubric: States that the grader check addresses classifier or scoring dependence only.
Identifies the weakness as scenario dependence: the two scenario halves agree only moderately (SB 0.70).

items.question: Why does it matter that the capability composite averages standardized rather than raw MMLU and GPQA scores?
items.answer: The two anchors spread models very differently: the between-model SD is 8.7 for MMLU and 18.2 for GPQA. A raw average would weight GPQA about twice as heavily in determining model differences. Standardizing gives each anchor equal weight.
rubric: States that a raw average would let GPQA dominate the composite.
Cites GPQA's roughly twice-larger between-model spread (SD 18.2 vs 8.7) and notes that standardizing equalizes the weights.

items.question: Under AIM alone, 11 of 22 models refuse every request. Why can the three-template average separate those 11 models?
items.answer: No model sits at the ceiling under the average, so each of the 11 must show at least some harmful compliance under refusal suppression or prefix injection. Those differing amounts of compliance break the ties that AIM alone leaves.
rubric: Infers that each AIM-ceiling model complies to some extent under at least one of the other two templates.
Explains that these differing compliance levels are what break the ties.

items.question: Prior work reports rank concordance near 0.10 across four agent-safety benchmarks on twelve models. Given this paper's power analysis, can that result distinguish benchmarks that are unrelated from benchmarks that are moderately related, and why?
items.answer: No. Even at n=18 the minimum detectable effect at 80% power is about ρ=0.62, and detecting ρ≈0.4 needs about 40 models. At 12 models, a true moderate correlation could easily yield an estimate near 0.10, and the panel sits at the paper's 'about a dozen' threshold for interpreting rank correlations at all.
rubric: Concludes that the result cannot distinguish no relation from a moderate relation.
Cites low power: minimum detectable effect about 0.62 at n=18 (worse at 12) and about 40 models needed for ρ≈0.4.

items.question: A team will build a shortlist of the safest quarter of models and wants it to be robust to which items happened to be sampled. Based on Table 3, would a shortlist drawn from AgentHarm or from the jailbreak outcome be more robust, and why?
items.answer: The jailbreak outcome. A top-quartile model stays top-quartile in 0.96 of resamples there, compared with 0.79 for AgentHarm, which has only 44 behaviors. Roughly one in five AgentHarm resamples would drop a shortlisted model, even though both instruments have similar split-half and rank stability.
rubric: Chooses the jailbreak outcome.
Cites top-quartile persistence of 0.96 versus 0.79 for AgentHarm.

items.question: A new reasoning model produces unstable long-form chain-of-thought on GPQA-Diamond. Following the paper's precedent, what is its status in the capability-adjusted analyses versus the chat-based outcome data?
items.answer: Like DeepSeek-R1, it would be excluded from the anchor panel, so it cannot enter capability-composite or rank-residualized analyses. It can still be scored on chat-based outcomes such as the jailbreak suite and included in their internal-consistency analysis, as DeepSeek-R1 was (42 models in Table 3).
rubric: States that it is excluded from the anchors and therefore from capability-adjusted analyses.
States that it can still be scored on, and included in the consistency analysis of, chat-based outcomes such as the jailbreak suite (the DeepSeek-R1 precedent).

items.question: A team argues that R-Judge is not capability-confounded because R-Judge specificity barely correlates with the capability composite. Per the paper, which other R-Judge summary must they examine before making that claim, and why?
items.answer: They should examine recall, and also F1 and balanced accuracy, which mix recall in. Recall rewards detecting unsafe content, which presupposes comprehension. Specificity can be achieved by a disposition to flag rarely. Capability content is a property of each summary, so a null on specificity does not transfer to the benchmark as a whole.
rubric: Names recall (or the recall-containing summaries F1 and balanced accuracy).
Explains that recall presupposes comprehension, while specificity can come from a disposition to flag rarely, so capability content is metric-specific.

items.question: A team wants to strengthen the misalignment outcome. Per the paper, should they collect more decisions within the existing blackmail and leaking scenarios or add scenarios, and why?
items.answer: They should add scenarios, along with replicate runs. The instrument's weakness is scenario dependence: the two halves agree only at Spearman–Brown 0.70. More decisions within the same two scenarios would shrink the binomial SE but would not address variation across scenarios. New scenarios should be pre-specified and should keep the probe specific to autonomous-agent misbehavior, unlike the severe-harm murder scenario.
rubric: Recommends adding scenarios (or replicates across scenarios) rather than only more decisions within the existing two.
Explains that the weakness is moderate cross-scenario agreement (SB 0.70), which within-scenario decisions do not address.

items.question: A new safety benchmark is scored by a multi-stage LLM-judge pipeline. Following the lesson of the paper's judge swaps, how should its judge-robustness check be designed?
items.answer: The check should re-run the full grading pipeline with a different judge rather than swapping only one component. The AgentHarm swap re-did only the refusal component and agreed less closely than the full-judge swaps on the misalignment and jailbreak outcomes, which reproduced model-level scores closely.
rubric: Recommends swapping or re-running the entire grading pipeline, not a single stage.
Cites the AgentHarm refusal-only swap agreeing less closely than the full swaps on misalignment and jailbreak.

items.question: If XSTest's unsafe subset had shown wide spread across models instead of 83–100% refusal (sd 4.5), which argument in the paper would lose force?
items.answer: The paper argues that overtly harmful single-turn prompts no longer separate current models, which is one reason agentic and jailbreak-based instruments are needed. A discriminating unsafe subset would undercut that motivation and would make the unsafe subset, not only the safe-subset over-refusal, informative.
rubric: Identifies the argument that single-turn harmful prompts no longer separate models, so agentic or jailbreak instruments are needed.
Explains that a discriminating unsafe subset would contradict the ceiling on which that argument rests.

items.question: If R-Judge specificity had shown low split-half consistency, around 0.5, instead of 0.99, which recommendation of the paper would be weakened, and why?
items.answer: The recommendation to report specificity alongside F1 as the complementary summary of the benign-trace error type would be weakened. If specificity were largely item-sampling noise, re-summarizing R-Judge under specificity (or a metric including it) would not reliably rank models for a monitor with costly false alarms.
rubric: Identifies the recommendation to report specificity (or full confusion-matrix complements) alongside F1.
Explains that an unreliable specificity would make specificity-based rankings mostly item-sampling noise.

items.question: If the 2,000-panel calibration check had shown the organization permutation test rejecting about 15% of the time at α=0.05 under the standard nulls, which analysis would lose its warrant?
items.answer: The organization-group comparison on the expanded panel would lose its warrant, because its p-values would overstate evidence of between-organization differences. The paper's statement that the test is adequately calibrated for panels of this shape would no longer hold.
rubric: Identifies the organization-group permutation comparison (or its calibration claim).
Explains that inflated Type-I error would make its significance overstate organization differences.

items.question: If AgentHarm had shown the weakest rather than the strongest held-out association with the jailbreak outcome, which interpretation would be challenged, and why?
items.answer: The paper reads the AgentHarm–jailbreak link as agreement between two instruments that both score harmful compliance. Weak agreement between two instruments aimed at a similar behavior would cast doubt on whether they measure that behavior consistently. It would point to a measurement problem, such as AgentHarm's grading or the jailbreak templates, rather than confirming convergence.
rubric: Identifies the reading of the association as agreement between two harmful-compliance instruments.
Explains that weak agreement between instruments aimed at the same behavior would suggest a measurement problem rather than convergence.

items.question: If the second misalignment grader (Claude-3-Haiku vs GPT-4o) had disagreed strongly at the model level, which conclusions would lose support?
items.answer: The claim that the misalignment outcome is not an artifact of a particular classifier would fail. Consequently, the capability–misalignment associations, both the original opposite association and its weakening on the expanded panel, could reflect the classifier rather than model behavior.
rubric: Identifies the claim that misalignment scores are robust to classifier or grader choice.
Notes that the capability–misalignment findings (original or expanded) would then be classifier-dependent.

items.question: If the harness had retained only each model's official R-Judge F1 rather than per-model verdicts and labels, which parts of the paper's analyses could not have been produced?
items.answer: Specificity, recall and balanced accuracy could not be computed, nor the constant-verdict reference rows. The R-Judge specificity row in Table 3 and the split-half and bootstrap analyses of R-Judge, which need item-level verdicts, would also be impossible, as would recomputing R-Judge quantities under alternative metrics.
rubric: Names the alternative metrics (specificity, recall, balanced accuracy) and/or the constant-verdict reference rows.
Notes that the item-level consistency analyses for R-Judge (Table 3 rows) also depend on stored per-item verdicts.

items.question: Does the paper show that R-Judge scores are unrelated to the misalignment outcome? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The pre-specified continuation on an intermediate n=25 panel did not meet its threshold and was stopped. At that size, moderate correlations such as ρ≈0.4 (which need about 40 models) are not reliably detectable, so the paper keeps the relationship only as a hypothesis.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Cites the stopped n=25 continuation together with low power (about 40 models needed for ρ≈0.4), so failure to meet the threshold is not evidence of no relation.

items.question: Does the paper show that high capability ensures jailbreak safety among current models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. On the expanded panel, jailbreak safety among high-capability models spans most of the scale. Capable models can therefore be either robust or highly vulnerable to the templates.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites that jailbreak safety among high-capability models spans most of the scale on the expanded panel.

items.question: Does the paper show that the audited agent-safety benchmarks share a single latent factor? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The PCA on 18 models and six columns is treated as a description of the sample, not a model of latent structure. Its eigenvalues are uncertain, and Pearson and Spearman conventions can retain different numbers of components. The passing negative control only shows that the pipeline does not create structure from noise.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Cites at least one of: small n=18 with limited resolution, convention sensitivity, the PCA being descriptive only, or the negative control testing only noise.

items.question: Does the paper show that its jailbreak outcome would rank models the same way under a different set of published jailbreak templates? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Only AIM, refusal suppression and prefix injection were used. Robustness checks covered base-prompt resampling and judge swaps, not template choice, and the AIM-only ceiling shows that template choice can change results substantially. Per-template scores are stored only so that such analyses can be run later.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that only three templates were tested, robustness checks did not vary templates, and/or the AIM ceiling shows results are template-sensitive.

items.question: Does the paper show that R-Judge's official F1 should be abandoned in favor of specificity? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper recommends reporting complementary metrics and constant-verdict reference rows alongside F1, not replacing it. The appropriate summary depends on the use case: a monitor with costly false alarms should prefer one that includes specificity, while a last-line filter may prefer recall.
rubric: Answers contradicted (or not supported).
Explains that the paper recommends reporting alternatives alongside F1, with metric choice depending on use case, such as recall for a last-line filter.

items.question: Does the paper show that its capability-adjusted correlations are insensitive to the choice between re-ranking rank residuals and taking Pearson correlations on unre-ranked rank residuals? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper states only that the two conventions coincide in large samples and differ slightly in small ones. It implements both so readers can check, but it reports no comparison showing that conclusions on its small panels are unchanged.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that the conventions differ in small samples and that both are implemented, but no result establishing insensitivity is reported.

items.question: A model has flagged some benign R-Judge traces. Extra benign traces are added to the dataset, and the model correctly passes all of them, with its other verdicts unchanged. Would its official F1 change?
items.answer: No. F1 combines recall and precision, and true negatives enter neither. Adding correctly passed benign traces adds only true negatives, so F1 is unchanged.
rubric: Answers no, F1 does not change.
Explains that the added traces are true negatives, which F1 ignores (recall and precision are unchanged).

items.question: A model has flagged some benign R-Judge traces. Extra benign traces are added to the dataset, and the model correctly passes all of them, with its other verdicts unchanged. Would its balanced accuracy change?
