items.answer: Yes, it would rise. Specificity, the fraction of benign traces correctly passed, increases when more benign traces are passed while the existing false positives stay fixed. Balanced accuracy averages specificity with performance on unsafe traces.
rubric: Answers yes, balanced accuracy increases.
Explains that specificity rises because true negatives increase while false positives are fixed, and balanced accuracy includes specificity.

items.question: Under the paper's pre-specified rule, would the common-panel PCA be interpreted if the capability anchors were the provider-reported MMLU and GPQA figures?
items.answer: No. The PCA is interpreted only if the positive and negative controls pass, and the positive control fails on provider-reported anchors.
rubric: Answers no.
Cites the rule that the PCA is interpreted only if the controls pass, together with the positive-control failure on provider numbers.

items.question: Under the paper's pre-specified rule, would the common-panel PCA be interpreted using the harmonized MMLU and GPQA anchors?
items.answer: Yes, as a descriptive summary of the sample. On the harmonized anchors the positive control passes, and the negative control also passes (median permuted eigenvalue 1.71 vs threshold 2.18), so the condition for interpretation is met.
rubric: Answers yes (descriptively).
Explains that both the positive control (harmonized anchors) and the negative control pass.

items.question: Could the 2026 expansion data be used to update the correlation between capability and jailbreak safety?
items.answer: Yes. The expansion re-measured both capability anchors and the jailbreak outcome under the original protocol on 41 anchored models.
rubric: Answers yes.
Notes that both the anchors and the jailbreak outcome were collected for the new models.

items.question: Could the 2026 expansion data be used to update the correlation between InjecAgent robustness and misalignment safety?
items.answer: No. The new models skipped the tool-calling audit benchmarks, and InjecAgent ran only on the original panel. The expansion therefore adds no InjecAgent scores to pair with the new misalignment scores.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that the audited benchmarks, including InjecAgent, were not run on the 2026 models.

items.question: Could InjecAgent robustness scores shift if the judge model used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?
items.answer: No. InjecAgent is rule-scored, so no judge model enters its scoring.
rubric: Answers no.
Explains that InjecAgent is rule-scored, with no judge model.

items.question: Could AgentHarm safety scores shift if its judge were replaced with a different LLM judge?
items.answer: Yes. AgentHarm is graded through a pipeline with a gpt-4o-mini judge, and re-scoring its refusal component with a Gemini judge agreed less closely than the judge swaps on the other outcomes.
rubric: Answers yes.
Cites AgentHarm's LLM-judge grading and the less close agreement of the refusal-judge swap.

items.question: Suppose the common-panel PCA retained a strong first component. Given the six columns it was run on, would that component by itself indicate a shared agent-safety construct, and why?
items.answer: No. Two of the six columns are the capability anchors, which the positive control shows agree with each other. Two more are R-Judge summaries computed from the same stored verdicts. Either pair could produce correlated columns, and so a retained component, without any shared safety construct.
rubric: Concludes that a retained component would not by itself show a shared safety construct

Notes that the columns include the two capability anchors (which agree, per the positive control) and/or two R-Judge summaries computed from the same verdicts, either of which can create covariance unrelated to safety

items.question: The worst-case within-model SEs are 13–25% of the between-model SD. Would that ratio still describe how well models can be told apart within a range-restricted group such as Anthropic's models near the safety ceiling, and why?
items.answer: No. The SDs come from the full expanded panel. Within a group packed near the ceiling, the spread is much smaller while the per-model SEs stay about the same, so the SEs would be a much larger share of the spread and models within the group may not be distinguishable.
rubric: Concludes that the ratio would not carry over to the range-restricted group
Explains that the SDs are computed over the full expanded panel, while the group's own spread is much smaller relative to unchanged per-model SEs

items.question: The jailbreak outcome's worst-case within-model SE is 3.7, bootstrapped over its ~150 judged units. Under what way of resampling those units would an SE like this understate the true uncertainty, and why?
items.answer: It would be too small if the ~150 units were resampled as independent items. They are 50 base prompts each judged under three templates, and the three templates applied to the same prompt are dependent, so treating them as independent overstates the effective sample size.
rubric: Identifies resampling the ~150 units independently rather than by base prompt as the problematic scheme
Explains that the three templates applied to the same base prompt are dependent, so independent resampling overstates the effective sample size and shrinks the SE

items.question: MMLU's internal consistency is computed on 356 of the 500 administered items. Is it guaranteed that the same split-half and rank-stability values would hold over all 500 items, and why?
items.answer: No. The 356 items are the intersection that every model answered. The excluded items are the ones at least one model failed to produce usable output on, so they may differ systematically from the rest. The consistency estimate strictly describes the shared subset.
rubric: Concludes that the values are not guaranteed for the full 500-item set
Explains that the analysis uses only the complete-coverage intersection, and the dropped items are selected by model failures, so they may not be a random subset

items.question: XSTest's safe subset is the paper's record of blanket refusal. Would it reveal a model that over-refuses benign requests only inside agentic, tool-using tasks, and why?
items.answer: Not reliably. XSTest is a prompt-level test of benign prompts that superficially resemble unsafe ones, run outside any tool loop. Over-refusal that appears only in agentic contexts, such as AgentHarm-style tasks, could therefore stay hidden inside high agentic safety scores.
rubric: Concludes that XSTest would not reliably reveal agentic-only over-refusal
Explains that XSTest measures prompt-level benign over-refusal outside the agentic tool setting, so behavior specific to that setting is not sampled

items.question: Under what kind of model-specific problem could the harmonized anchors pass the positive control and still give that model a misleading capability composite, and why?
items.answer: A model-specific harness or parsing problem that depresses both MMLU and GPQA together, because both anchors run through the same API harness. The two anchors would then agree, so the positive control passes, while both understate the model's ability. Only telemetry gates on usable output guard against this.
rubric: Identifies a model-specific harness, parsing or output problem that affects both anchors in the same direction
Explains that the positive control only checks agreement between the anchors, so a shared distortion preserves agreement while biasing the composite

items.question: In the negative control, 2% of the column-permuted matrices exceed the parallel-analysis threshold. Why is this reassuring rather than a sign of spurious structure?
items.answer: The threshold is the 95th percentile of the random-normal null, so about 5% of structure-free matrices would be expected to exceed it by chance. An exceedance of 2%, with a median first eigenvalue of 1.71 against 2.18, is no higher than chance, so the pipeline is not creating structure from noise.
rubric: Concludes that the 2% exceedance is consistent with no spurious structure
Explains that the threshold is a 95th-percentile null value, so roughly 5% exceedance is expected by chance and 2% does not exceed that

items.question: Why would adding AgentDojo as a column in the common-panel PCA make the analysis worse rather than more complete?
items.answer: The PCA needs every model to have a score on every column. AgentDojo covers only 5 models, so the shared set would fall from 18 to at most 5. That is far below the roughly a dozen models the paper requires before interpreting rank relationships.
rubric: States that including AgentDojo would shrink the analyzable panel to at most 5 models
Links this to the need for complete rows across columns and the paper's minimum of about a dozen models

items.question: GLM-4.5 produced a valid MMLU score. Why can it still not enter any capability-adjusted analysis?
items.answer: The capability composite is the mean of the standardized MMLU and GPQA anchors. GLM-4.5 has no GPQA score, so no composite can be formed for it. It therefore appears only as a partial row in Figure 3.
rubric: States that the model has no capability composite
Explains that the composite requires both standardized MMLU and GPQA, and GLM-4.5 lacks GPQA

items.question: The pre-specified R-Judge/misalignment continuation on an n=25 intermediate panel missed its threshold. Why does the paper keep it as a hypothesis rather than treat it as evidence that no relationship exists?
items.answer: At n=25 the panel is still underpowered for moderate correlations. A ρ of about 0.4 needs roughly 40 models for 80% power, and even n=18 only detects about 0.62. Failing to reach the threshold is therefore uninformative about a moderate true relationship.
rubric: Concludes that the miss does not show the absence of a relationship
Cites low power: about 40 models are needed for ρ≈0.4, and n=25 falls well short

items.question: The InjecAgent–AgentDojo convergent control is inconclusive. Why does that not prevent the common-panel PCA from being interpreted under the paper's pre-specified rule?
items.answer: The rule makes PCA interpretation conditional only on the positive and negative controls, and both pass. AgentDojo is not one of the PCA columns. The inconclusive convergent control therefore leaves the condition for interpretation untouched.
rubric: States that the PCA can still be interpreted
Explains that the rule requires only the positive and negative controls to pass, both of which do, and/or that AgentDojo is not a PCA column

items.question: Why would correlating an AIM-only jailbreak score with other refusal-based instruments tend to understate any association that exists?
items.answer: Under AIM alone, 11 of 22 models refuse every request and tie at the ceiling. Whatever ordering those models have on the other instruments cannot be matched by the jailbreak scores. The tied half of the panel adds noise to the rank correlation and weakens it.
rubric: Concludes that the AIM-only score would attenuate (understate) the association
Explains that half the panel ties at the ceiling, so differences among those models cannot contribute to the rank correlation

items.question: The paper gives 0.5^4 ≈ 6.2% as the chance that one coder matches all four labels by coin flip. What is the analogous chance baseline for one coder matching all six targets in the distractor round, and why is it smaller?
items.answer: About (1/3)^6 ≈ 0.14%, because each of the six targets now has three possible constructs. With more options per target and more targets, matching every label by chance is far less likely than 6.2%, which is why the round is more demanding.
rubric: Gives approximately (1/3)^6, about 0.14% (or an equivalent expression)
Explains that three constructs per target and six targets make a chance match much less likely than in the two-construct, four-benchmark round

items.question: A reader applies a Bonferroni correction to the released R-Judge analyses. What does following the paper's recommendation to report specificity, recall, balanced accuracy and F1 do to that correction, compared with reporting official F1 alone?
items.answer: It multiplies the number of R-Judge-involving tests by about four, which makes the per-test threshold stricter. The paper warns that the number of tests grows quickly with the number of metrics reported per benchmark. Reporting all four summaries is therefore a trade-off against family-wise power.
rubric: States that the correction becomes stricter because the number of tests roughly quadruples
Ties this to the paper's warning that the test count grows with the number of metrics reported per benchmark

items.question: Two teams analyze the same 18-model score matrix. One uses the Pearson convention, the other the Spearman convention, and they retain different numbers of components. Per the paper, does this mean one team made an error, and what should they report?
items.answer: Not necessarily. With bounded, skewed instruments and a small panel, the two conventions can legitimately retain different numbers of components. Both should be reported, and the factor analysis should be treated as supporting rather than primary evidence.
rubric: Concludes that the discrepancy does not imply an error
Explains that convention sensitivity is expected on small panels with bounded, skewed scores, so both conventions should be reported and the PCA treated as supporting evidence

items.question: A new organization contributes two anchored models to an expanded panel. Can it be one of the groups in the paper's permutation-test comparison of organizations, and why?
items.answer: No. The pre-specified comparison includes only organization groups with at least three models. Its two models can still appear in pooled analyses, but the organization cannot form a comparison group.
rubric: Concludes that the organization cannot be a comparison group
Cites the requirement of at least three models per organization group

items.question: A team plans a cross-benchmark study and wants 80% power at α=0.05 to detect a true Spearman correlation of about 0.5. Based on the paper's power figures, roughly how large must its panel be?
items.answer: Larger than 18 but smaller than about 40. At n=18 the minimum detectable effect is about 0.62, above 0.5, while about 40 models are needed for 0.4. A target of 0.5 therefore needs a panel somewhere in between, in the high 20s or 30s.
rubric: Gives a size between about 18 and about 40 (more than the n=18 common panel)
Justifies this from n=18 detecting only ρ≈0.62 and ρ≈0.4 needing about 40 models

items.question: After the study, a team uses the stored per-template jailbreak scores to test whether prefix injection alone predicts AgentHarm safety. How should that result be treated under the paper's practices?
items.answer: As exploratory, because the primary pre-specified outcome is the three-template average and a single-template analysis is outside the plan. The team should also check that template for ceilings, since a single template can saturate, as AIM did.
rubric: States that the result is exploratory (not pre-specified) because the primary outcome is the three-template average
Notes the need to check the single template for a ceiling effect, as with AIM

items.question: If the harmonized capability composite had shown no association with τ² task success, which role the paper assigns to τ² would be undermined?
items.answer: Its role as the reference outcome that capability is expected to explain, against which the safety outcomes are read. If capability failed to track task success, either the composite or the τ² measurement would be suspect. Contrasting the safety outcomes with τ² would then lose its anchor.
rubric: Identifies τ²'s role as the reference outcome that capability should explain
Explains that without that association the contrast with the safety outcomes, and confidence in the composite or τ², would be undermined

items.question: If R-Judge specificity, recall, balanced accuracy and F1 had ordered the models identically, which of the paper's arguments would lose its practical force?
items.answer: The argument that metric choice is part of the claim: that R-Judge's capability content differs by summary and secondary analyses should report the alternatives. If all summaries gave the same ranking, the choice of summary would not change conclusions in practice.
rubric: Identifies the argument that capability content and conclusions depend on which R-Judge summary is used (metric choice is part of the claim)
Explains that identical rankings would leave no case in which the summary choice changes conclusions

items.question: If the impressions formed on the first seven-model panel had held up on the full n=18 common panel, which recommendation would lose its first-hand motivating evidence?
items.answer: The recommendation to treat small-panel relationships as provisional, show subsampling variability and avoid interpreting rank correlations on fewer than about a dozen models. The authors' own failed n=7 impressions are their direct example of the hazard.
rubric: Identifies the recommendation to treat small-panel correlations as provisional, report subsampling variability, and avoid interpreting fewer than about a dozen models
Explains that the non-persistence of the n=7 impressions is the paper's first-hand demonstration of that hazard

items.question: If the harness had measured only one capability anchor (say MMLU), which of the pre-specified harness controls could not have been run at all?
items.answer: The positive control, because it is defined as the capability anchors agreeing with one another. With a single anchor there is no second measure to agree with, so the comparison between provider-reported and harmonized anchors on this control could not have been made.
rubric: Identifies the positive control
Explains that it requires agreement between two anchors, which is impossible with only one

items.question: Per-model SEs for the jailbreak outcome are reported to be small. If its top-quartile persistence had nonetheless come out low, which statement in the paper would that illustrate?
items.answer: That small SEs do not by themselves make rankings stable, which is the stated reason internal consistency is computed in addition to precision. Precise per-model scores can still give a top group that reshuffles under item resampling when models are close.
rubric: Identifies the statement that small SEs alone do not guarantee stable rankings (the motivation for the consistency analyses)
Explains that rankings can reshuffle under item resampling even when individual scores are precise

items.question: Does Table 3 show that every item-rich instrument has an uncorrected split-half correlation of at least 0.96? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Only R-Judge specificity reaches 0.98 uncorrected; the others are 0.93–0.95. The ≥0.96 figure refers to Spearman–Brown corrected values, which project the consistency of the full-length instrument.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that most uncorrected values are 0.93–0.95 and the ≥0.96 threshold applies to Spearman–Brown corrected values

items.question: Does the paper show that error in the capability covariate can only weaken, never inflate, its capability-adjusted relationships? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper says covariate measurement error attenuates or distorts adjusted relationships in directions that are hard to sign. Adjusted estimates could therefore be biased either way, not only toward zero.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites the paper's statement that covariate error attenuates or distorts adjusted relationships in hard-to-sign directions

items.question: Does the paper show that more capable models are, in general, more prone to agentic misalignment? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The opposite-direction association comes from the original panel and weakens on the 41-model expansion. The outcome is a single fictional-scenario probe whose halves agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70), and capability is a static composite. The claim does not generalize from this evidence.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites at least one of: the weakening on the expanded panel, the fictional single-scenario probe with only moderate half agreement, or the static capability composite

items.question: Does the paper's InjecAgent evidence establish model rankings for prompt-injection robustness in general? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. InjecAgent was run on 300 rule-scored items stratified across only the direct-harm and data-stealing categories. Its convergent check against AgentDojo is inconclusive at n=5. High internal consistency shows stable rankings on these items, not across injection types generally.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites the restricted item set (direct-harm and data-stealing items) and/or the inconclusive convergent control, noting that internal consistency covers only this item set

items.question: Does the paper show that current models no longer differ in how they refuse harmful requests? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Only the XSTest unsafe subset of overtly harmful prompts is ceilinged (83–100%). Under the three-template jailbreak suite, safety among high-capability expanded-panel models spans most of the scale, so models still differ under jailbreak pressure.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Contrasts the ceilinged overtly-harmful XSTest subset with the wide spread on the three-template jailbreak outcome

items.question: Does the paper show that BFCL is an invalid benchmark of function-calling ability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper reports only a six-model pilot showing that BFCL failed as an agentic replacement for the capability covariate, apparently rewarding format conformance. That is a narrow finding about its use as a covariate on this panel, not a general verdict on the benchmark.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the evidence is a six-model pilot about its suitability as a capability covariate (format conformance), not a general validity test

items.question: An organization-group permutation test on the misalignment outcome gives p≈0.04. Is this result exposed to the false-positive inflation found under the worst-case clustered-variance null?
items.answer: No. The worst-case inflation appeared on the jailbreak structure only. Rejection rates for misalignment matched nominal α (0.045–0.052 at α=0.05).
rubric: Answers no
Notes that the worst-case inflation was found only on the jailbreak structure, with misalignment calibrated at nominal levels

items.question: An organization-group permutation test on the jailbreak outcome gives p≈0.04. Is this result exposed to the false-positive inflation found under the worst-case clustered-variance null?
items.answer: Yes, to a mild degree. Under the worst-case null the jailbreak test rejects about 6.7% of the time at α=0.05, so a result near 0.05 is less secure. Only at α=0.005 was no inflation detected.
rubric: Answers yes (mildly)
Cites the 0.067 rejection rate at α=0.05 on jailbreak, with no inflation only at the stricter α=0.005

items.question: An agent appears injection-robust only because it rarely completes any requested task. Would AgentDojo's scoring expose this?
items.answer: Yes. AgentDojo is environment-scored for utility as well as security, so an agent that does little would show low utility alongside its high security.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that AgentDojo scores utility as well as security

items.question: An agent appears injection-robust only because it rarely completes any requested task. Would InjecAgent's robustness score expose this?
items.answer: No. InjecAgent robustness is rule-scored as one minus attack success and has no utility component. An agent that rarely acts would simply show low attack success and look robust.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that InjecAgent scores only attack success (robustness = 1 − attack success), with no utility measure

items.question: Would running each model on τ²-retail several more times allow a within-model uncertainty bound to be placed on its τ² score?
items.answer: Yes. The missing bound comes from user-simulator variance, which a single run cannot capture. Replicate runs would expose run-to-run variation from which an SE could be estimated.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that the obstacle is user-simulator variance across runs, which replicate runs make observable

items.question: Would re-scoring each model's existing τ²-retail final database states a second time allow a within-model uncertainty bound to be placed on its τ² score?
items.answer: No. τ² success is environment-scored from the final database state and does not depend on a judge, so re-scoring would reproduce the same result. The variance comes from the user simulator during the single run, which re-scoring cannot reveal.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that environment scoring is judge-free, so re-scoring reproduces the same result, while the unbounded variance comes from the simulator during the run

items.question: Could a model with poor comprehension of interaction traces still achieve high R-Judge specificity?
items.answer: Yes. Specificity rewards leaving benign traces alone, which a disposition to rarely flag anything achieves without understanding the traces.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that specificity can be achieved by a disposition to flag rarely, without comprehension

items.question: Could a model with poor comprehension of interaction traces still achieve high R-Judge balanced accuracy?
items.answer: No. Balanced accuracy weights benign and unsafe traces equally, so it also requires high recall on unsafe traces. Catching unsafe content without flagging everything presupposes comprehension, and a rarely-flagging disposition would score low on recall.
rubric: Answers no
Explains that balanced accuracy also requires recall on unsafe traces, which presupposes comprehension (a rarely-flagging disposition fails on recall)

items.question: Could models' R-Judge F1 scores shift if the gpt-4o-mini judge used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?
items.answer: No. R-Judge is run as a self-judge benchmark: the score compares each model's own safe/unsafe verdict with the record's label, so no external judge model enters the scoring.
rubric: Asserts that R-Judge F1 would not shift (no / unaffected).
Reason: R-Judge is self-judged; verdicts are compared directly against labels, with no external LLM judge in the scoring.

items.question: Could models' XSTest safe-subset over-refusal rates shift if the gpt-4o-mini judge used elsewhere in the harness were replaced with a different LLM judge?
items.answer: Yes. XSTest is scored with the published CPI (compliance/partial/refusal) scorer, which uses gpt-4o-mini as its judge. Changing the judge can change which responses count as refusals.
rubric: Asserts that the rates could shift (yes).
Reason: XSTest's CPI scorer relies on a gpt-4o-mini judge to classify responses as compliance, partial or refusal.

items.question: Suppose Gemini-2.5-Pro, which yielded no valid capability anchor, had nonetheless had its jailbreak responses fully judged. Could it be included in the jailbreak row of the internal-consistency table (Table 3)?
items.answer: Yes. The consistency computation needs only item-level jailbreak data, not anchors. The paper already includes DeepSeek-R1, which lacks the anchor pair, which is why that row has 42 models. Gemini-2.5-Pro would need judged responses on the shared base prompts so that the common prompt set does not shrink.
rubric: Asserts yes, it could be included.
Reason: internal consistency uses only the instrument's item-level data, and DeepSeek-R1 was included without an anchor pair (42 models).
Condition: its judged prompts must cover the shared prompt set, or the intersection would shrink.

items.question: Under the same supposition (Gemini-2.5-Pro jailbreak responses fully judged, no valid anchor), could Gemini-2.5-Pro enter the expanded-panel correlation between capability and jailbreak safety?
items.answer: No. That analysis uses the 41 anchored models and needs each model's harmonized capability composite. A model with no valid MMLU/GPQA anchor has no composite, so it cannot be placed on the capability axis.
rubric: Asserts no.
Reason: capability analyses require the harmonized anchor composite, and the expanded analyses are restricted to anchored models; Gemini-2.5-Pro has no valid anchor.

items.question: If MMLU were administered on 1,000 fixed items instead of 500, would its worst-case within-model SE be expected to fall?
items.answer: Yes. The MMLU SE is binomial, so it shrinks with the square root of the item count. The worst case would fall from about 2.2 to about 1.6 points.
rubric: Asserts yes, the worst-case SE would fall.
Reason: a binomial SE scales with 1/sqrt(number of items), so doubling the items lowers it (to roughly 1.6 points).

items.question: If MMLU were administered on 1,000 fixed items instead of 500, would its between-model SD (8.7) be expected to fall correspondingly?
items.answer: No. The between-model SD mainly reflects real differences in model accuracy, which more items do not remove; only the small item-noise component would shrink. The SE-to-SD ratio would therefore improve.
rubric: Asserts no, the between-model SD would not fall correspondingly (it would stay roughly the same).
Reason: the SD reflects true spread among models rather than item-sampling noise, so only the SE shrinks and the SE/SD ratio improves.

items.question: In the PCA negative control, if each score column is permuted independently across models, does the permutation destroy any between-column correlation present in the real data?
items.answer: Yes. Shuffling each column separately breaks the link between a model's score on one instrument and its scores on the others. Any real covariance structure is removed, which is what makes the result a null against which to check the pipeline.
rubric: Asserts yes.
Reason: independent shuffling of each column decouples models' scores across instruments, so any genuine correlation structure is removed and the result is a valid null.

items.question: If instead the same reordering of models were applied to every column jointly, would the permutation destroy any between-column correlation present in the real data?
items.answer: No. A joint permutation only relabels the rows. Each model keeps its full set of scores, so the correlation matrix and its eigenvalues are identical to the real data's, and the result cannot serve as a null.
rubric: Asserts no.
Reason: applying one permutation to all columns just reorders models while keeping each model's scores together, so the correlations and eigenvalues are unchanged.

items.question: Why does the paper run its organization-group analysis (permutation test over organizations with at least three models) only on the expanded panel and not on the original 22-model roster?
items.answer: On the original roster only four organizations have three or more models (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3), and only OpenAI has four or more. The other five organizations contribute one or two models each. That leaves too few clusters and too few models per cluster for a group comparison. The expanded panel has seven organizations with three or more models and six with four or more.
rubric: Concludes that the original roster has too few organizations with enough models for the group comparison.

Reason: only four original organizations reach three models (OpenAI 6, Meta, Qwen, Mistral 3) and only OpenAI reaches four, whereas the expanded panel has seven with three or more and six with four or more.

items.question: Why are both the median first eigenvalue of the column-permuted matrices (1.71) and the parallel-analysis threshold (2.18) well above 1, even though the permuted columns are unrelated by construction?
items.answer: With only 18 models and six columns, sampling noise alone produces sizeable chance correlations among unrelated columns. The largest eigenvalue of such data therefore lands well above 1. This is why the paper compares eigenvalues with a simulated random-normal null rather than with a fixed cutoff, and why it notes that eigenvalues on this panel carry substantial sampling uncertainty.
rubric: Concludes that eigenvalues above 1 are expected even for unrelated columns.
Reason: with small n (18 models), chance correlations from sampling noise inflate the largest eigenvalue, which is why a simulated parallel-analysis null is used instead of a fixed threshold.

items.question: GPQA's median within-model SE (3.3) is close to its maximum (3.6), while MMLU's median (1.6) is well below its maximum (2.2). Why the difference, given that both are binomial SEs?
items.answer: A binomial SE peaks when accuracy is near 50%; 2.2 and 3.6 are roughly the maxima for 500 and 198 items. A median close to the maximum means most models score in the mid range on GPQA. MMLU's much lower median means most models score far from 50%, at high accuracy, with only a few near the middle.
rubric: Concludes that most models sit near mid-range accuracy on GPQA but well above it on MMLU.
Reason: a binomial SE is largest at about 50% accuracy and smaller toward the extremes, so the median-to-maximum gap reflects where models' accuracies fall.

items.question: The four audited benchmarks order models differently on the common panel. Why does the paper hold that this disagreement does not by itself indict any single benchmark?
items.answer: Before collecting any scores, the benchmarks were assigned to different target behaviors: R-Judge and the injection benchmarks to risk recognition, and AgentHarm to harm blocking. Blinded coders recovered these assignments. Instruments aimed at different behaviors have no reason to rank models identically. What the disagreement does undercut is quoting them interchangeably as 'the safety' of an agent.
rubric: Concludes that disagreement is expected rather than evidence that a benchmark is faulty.

Reason: the benchmarks target different behaviors (pre-specified targets that blinded coders recovered), so their rankings need not agree; what the disagreement undermines is interchangeable use of the scores.

items.question: The expanded analyses use 41 anchored models, yet the MMLU row of the internal-consistency table covers 46 models. Why?
items.answer: The extra rows are models that have MMLU item logs but were excluded from the anchored panel, for example DeepSeek-R1 (unstable GPQA) and GLM-4.5 (MMLU but no GPQA). Internal consistency is a property of the instrument and needs only item-level data. It does not require the full anchor pair or passing the gates needed for capability-adjusted analyses.
rubric: Concludes that the 46 include models outside the 41-model anchored panel, such as DeepSeek-R1 and GLM-4.5, that have MMLU item logs.
Reason: consistency is computed from the instrument's own item data and does not require a complete anchor composite or inclusion in capability analyses.

items.question: InjecAgent covers all 22 models, while AgentHarm covers 19 and AgentDojo only 5. Why?
items.answer: AgentHarm and AgentDojo require native tool calling. Models whose provider interface lacks the required schema are recorded as not-run rather than forced through an emulation layer, because emulation would change the instrument. InjecAgent is rule-scored and does not depend on native tool support, so every model can be run.
rubric: Concludes that the coverage gap comes from the native tool-calling requirement.
Reason: AgentHarm and AgentDojo need native tool use, and unsupported models are not-run rather than emulated, whereas InjecAgent has no such requirement.

items.question: Why does the split-half computation share each random half-split across all models, using only items common to every model's logs, rather than drawing separate splits per model?
items.answer: Sharing the splits means every model's half-score rests on exactly the same items. The correlation between halves then measures whether different item subsets order the models consistently. With per-model splits, models would be scored on different items, and differences in item difficulty would mix into the comparison.
rubric: Concludes that shared splits are needed so that the comparison is of rankings on identical items.
Reason: per-model splits would put models on different items, confounding ranking consistency with differences in item difficulty.

items.question: AgentHarm and XSTest are both scored with gpt-4o-mini judges. Under what condition would an association between XSTest safe-subset over-refusal and AgentHarm safety be produced by scoring rather than by model behavior, and why?
items.answer: This would happen if gpt-4o-mini systematically labels some response style (for example hedged or partial answers) as refusal. A model that writes in that style would be scored as refusing on both instruments, creating shared judge variance that looks like a behavioral link. The paper's AgentHarm refusal-judge swap agreed less closely, so judge choice is not innocuous for that instrument.
rubric: Identifies the condition: a systematic gpt-4o-mini bias toward classifying certain response styles as refusals.
Reason: because both instruments share that judge, the bias would move both scores in the same direction (shared method variance) and produce a spurious association.

items.question: The paper's within-model SEs were computed from existing item-level data with no new runs. Would they capture how much a model's score could change if the same model were rerun on the same items, and why?
items.answer: No. The SEs are binomial or bootstrap quantities over item sampling. They do not include run-to-run decoding stochasticity, judge noise on new completions, or simulator variance. A rerun could therefore shift scores by more than these SEs suggest. τ²'s single run is the paper's own example of variance it cannot bound.
rubric: Asserts no.
Reason: the SEs reflect only item-sampling variability from one set of completions, not variation across repeated runs (decoding, judge or simulator noise).

items.question: Suppose the 2026 models' jailbreak responses had been scored with the Gemini judge while the original panel kept the gpt-4o judge. Would comparing the capability–jailbreak correlation across panels remain clean, and why?
items.answer: Not fully. Judge identity would be confounded with panel membership, so part of any change could come from scoring rather than from the models. The Gemini swap reproduced model-level scores closely, which suggests the distortion would be modest. The paper avoided the issue by rescoring new models with the same judge and the same base prompts.
rubric: Asserts that the comparison would be compromised (not clean).
Reason: the judge would differ systematically between original and new models, confounding judge with panel.
Nuance: the close Gemini/gpt-4o agreement suggests any distortion would likely be small.

items.question: The misalignment outcome's two scenario halves give Spearman–Brown 0.70. Would a Spearman–Brown projection from this figure reliably predict the consistency of the three-scenario battery that adds the murder scenario, and why?
items.answer: No. The Spearman–Brown projection assumes the added parts are comparable to the existing ones. The murder scenario differs in kind: it involves severe harm that harm-compliance instruments may anticipate. Adding it changes what is measured rather than simply lengthening the same instrument.
rubric: Asserts no.

Reason: the projection assumes comparable parts, but the murder scenario differs in kind (severe harm also anticipated by harm-compliance instruments), so it changes the construct rather than adding parallel items.

items.question: Suppose the XSTest comparison panel showed a sizeable rank correlation between safe-subset over-refusal and an audited benchmark. Would it be robust to leaving out individual models, and why?
items.answer: Probably not. Most of the over-refusal variation comes from two models, Claude-3-Haiku at 60% and o3-mini at 30%, while every other model sits at 15% or below. On n=17–20, a single unusual model can drive a rank correlation, so dropping one of those two could change it substantially.
rubric: Asserts that it would likely be fragile, not robust.

Reason: the over-refusal spread is concentrated in Claude-3-Haiku (60%) and o3-mini (30%), with the rest at 15% or below, and on a panel of about 17–20 models single models can drive rank correlations.

items.question: The jailbreak outcome uses three published templates applied to a fixed set of forbidden prompts. Under what condition would high scores from newer models stop indicating jailbreak robustness, and why?
items.answer: This would happen if newer models had been trained against these specific published templates or prompts. Their refusals would then reflect exposure to the test items rather than general robustness. The paper names training on test items as a form of gaming, and the outcome includes no adaptive attacks that would reveal the gap.
rubric: Identifies the condition: newer models trained on or tuned against these published templates/prompts (test-item exposure).
Reason: scores would then reflect familiarity with the fixed items rather than robustness, and the outcome has no adaptive attacks to detect this.

items.question: The misalignment SE treats each model's 100 decisions as binomial. Why could this understate that model's true within-model uncertainty?
items.answer: The 100 decisions come from only two scenario configurations, and the data are config-level, so decisions within a scenario are likely dependent rather than independent draws. The two halves agree only moderately (Spearman–Brown 0.70), which indicates scenario-specific variance. A binomial SE over 100 independent decisions ignores this variance.
rubric: Concludes that the binomial SE can be too small.
Reason: decisions are clustered in just two scenarios (config-level data), so they are not independent, and the moderate halves agreement points to scenario variance that the binomial formula omits.

items.question: On the original 22-model roster, which single organization's removal in a leave-one-organization-out check would change the panel most, and why is that check needed for it specifically?
items.answer: OpenAI's. Removing its 6 models takes out about 27% of the panel and leaves 16. Because those six models share training pipelines and safety tuning, they could jointly drive an estimate in a way that removing one model at a time would not reveal.
rubric: Names OpenAI (6 of 22 models, leaving 16).
Reason: its models share pipelines and tuning, so they can jointly drive an estimate that leave-one-model-out cannot detect.

items.question: A team proposes a held-out harm outcome for current models made of overtly harmful single-turn prompts with no jailbreak template, scored by refusal. What should they expect, based on the paper?
items.answer: They should expect a ceiling with little discriminating variance. On XSTest's unsafe subset every model refuses 83–100% (sd 4.5), and even a single jailbreak template (AIM) left 11 of 22 models refusing everything. The paper's lesson is to check for ceilings first and to prefer multi-template or agentic designs.
rubric: Predicts a ceiling or near-ceiling with little discrimination among models.
Reason: cites XSTest's unsafe subset (83–100% refusal, sd 4.5) and/or the AIM-only ceiling (11/22 refuse every request), and recommends ceiling checks or multi-template/agentic designs.

items.question: A team reproduces the paper's MMLU protocol but draws a fresh random 500-item subset for each model. What does this undermine?
items.answer: Models are no longer scored on identical items. Score differences then partly reflect item difficulty, which breaks the uniform protocol the anchors rely on. It also removes most of the shared item base needed for the common-item split-half and rank-stability computations.
rubric: Concludes that comparability across models (the uniform protocol) is undermined.
Reason: different items per model mean score differences partly reflect item difficulty, and the common-item consistency analyses lose their shared item base.

items.question: A team wants to add AgentHarm scores for the paper's 41-model expanded panel. What panel should they expect, and why?
items.answer: They should expect fewer than 41 models, and a non-random subset. AgentHarm needs native tool calling, and unsupported models are not-run rather than emulated. Coverage loss falls disproportionately on models with non-standard tool interfaces, and several 2026 models already hit routing incompatibilities with the harness.
rubric: Predicts a panel smaller than 41 and non-randomly selected.
Reason: AgentHarm requires native tool use without emulation, coverage loss concentrates on non-standard interfaces, and the harness was already stale for some 2026 models.

items.question: A team builds a capability composite from harness-measured MMLU/GPQA for most models but fills in provider-reported figures for a few models that are hard to run. What is wrong with this, per the paper?
items.answer: Mixing sources reintroduces heterogeneous prompts, shot counts and decoding settings for those models, so their composite partly reflects reporting practice. Provider figures failed the positive control. The paper's practice is to measure every anchor under its own protocol, or to exclude models that cannot be measured, as it did with Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-R1.
rubric: Concludes that the mixed composite is not comparable across models and should not be used.
Reason: provider figures come from heterogeneous conditions and failed the positive control; models should be measured under the uniform protocol or excluded.

items.question: A team wants 80% power at α=0.05 to detect a true Spearman correlation near 0.4 between AgentHarm and InjecAgent. Starting from the n=18 common panel, roughly how many models must they add, and what practical obstacle will they face?
items.answer: They need to add roughly 22 models, to reach about 40. Every added model must support native tool calling for AgentHarm. That is hard because coverage loss concentrates on models with non-standard tool interfaces and harnesses go stale as interfaces change.
rubric: States roughly 22 more models (to about 40 total).
Reason/obstacle: each must run AgentHarm with native tool calling, and coverage loss on non-standard interfaces and harness staleness make this difficult.

items.question: If Llama-3.3-70B's dissenting view (InjecAgent as harm blocking) had been the coders' majority, which pre-specified harness control would lose its rationale?
items.answer: The convergent control. It assumes InjecAgent and AgentDojo target the same construct, and coders placed AgentDojo unanimously under risk recognition. If InjecAgent were read as harm blocking, there would be no basis for expecting the two to agree.
rubric: Names the convergent (InjecAgent–AgentDojo) control.
Reason: that control presumes both benchmarks share a construct; coding InjecAgent as harm blocking while AgentDojo is coded recognition removes the expectation of agreement.

items.question: If the audited benchmarks' split-half consistency had been low (around 0.5) instead of 0.96 or above, how would the interpretation of their cross-benchmark disagreement change?
items.answer: The disagreement could then be explained by item-sampling noise within each instrument rather than by the instruments genuinely ranking models differently. High internal consistency is what makes item-sampling error an unlikely source of instability in rankings, so the disagreement can be read as substantive.
rubric: Concludes that the disagreement could be attributed to measurement noise rather than real differences between instruments.
Reason: high split-half and rank stability are what rule out item-sampling error as the source of ranking differences.

items.question: If the AIM template alone had not produced a ceiling (models spread across the scale), which Discussion recommendation would lose its direct demonstration in this audit, and which part would still have support?
items.answer: The recommendation to prefer multi-template designs where a single template saturates would lose its first-hand case, since the three-template average was adopted to fix the AIM ceiling. The broader advice to check outcomes for ceilings would still be supported by the ceilinged XSTest unsafe subset (83–100% refusal).
rubric: Names the multi-template part of the fourth recommendation (prefer multi-template designs when a single template saturates) as losing its direct evidence.
Notes that ceiling-checking remains supported by the ceilinged XSTest unsafe subset.

items.question: If the Gemini refusal-judge rescoring of AgentHarm had agreed closely with the original grading, which aspect of judge robustness would it support, and which would remain untested?
items.answer: It would support robustness of the refusal component to judge choice. It would not test the rest of AgentHarm's multi-stage grading pipeline, which was not redone. Robustness of full AgentHarm scores to the judge would therefore remain unestablished.
rubric: States that it would support robustness of the refusal component only.
Reason: the swap redoes only the refusal stage, so the other grading stages, and hence full-score robustness, remain untested.

items.question: Suppose the models lost from AgentHarm coverage because of non-standard tool interfaces had been disproportionately the most capable. Which common-panel results would be most distorted, and why?
items.answer: Relationships between the audited benchmarks and capability would be most distorted. The common panel would be range-restricted on capability, which can weaken or distort those associations. The results would also not carry over to the excluded, more capable models.
rubric: Identifies capability-related associations on the common panel (benchmark versus capability, or capability-adjusted analyses).
Reason: non-random loss would range-restrict capability and bias associations, and limit generalization to the excluded models.

items.question: If the murder scenario had been part of the pre-specified primary misalignment outcome from the start, which objection to using the three-scenario battery would disappear, and which would remain?
items.answer: The forking-path objection would disappear, because it arises only from adding the scenario after the primary outcome was fixed. The dilution objection would remain: murder involves severe harm that harm-compliance instruments may also anticipate, which weakens the probe's specificity to autonomous-agent misbehavior.
rubric: States that the forking-path (post hoc addition) objection would disappear.
States that the loss of specificity would remain, because murder's severe harm overlaps with what harm-compliance instruments capture.

items.question: Does the paper show that agent-safety benchmark scores are too noisy to rank models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The item-rich instruments have split-half of at least 0.96 and rank stability of at least 0.97, and worst-case SEs are only 13–25% of between-model spread. Panel-level rankings are therefore not dominated by noise. The caveats are that closely scored pairs can fall within their SEs and that the single-scenario and single-run outcomes are weaker.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: high internal consistency (split-half ≥0.96, rank stability ≥0.97) and SEs that are a small fraction of between-model SD.
Caveat: close pairs and the misalignment/τ² outcomes are exceptions.

items.question: Does the paper show that the cross-benchmark ranking disagreement reported in prior work (concordance near 0.10) arises entirely from heterogeneous evaluation harnesses? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Run under one harness on a common panel, the benchmarks still disagree. They also target different behaviors, which blinded coding confirms, so some disagreement is expected regardless of harness. Low power at n=18 limits how precisely the disagreement can be sized.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: disagreement persists under a single harness on a common panel, and the benchmarks target different constructs.

items.question: Does the paper show that a fixed evaluation harness keeps working reliably as new models are released? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. In the 2026 expansion several newer models could not be run reliably through the same interface. Gemini-2.5-Pro yielded no valid anchor and GLM-4.5 only partial anchors, both because of routing incompatibilities. The paper presents these as instances of harnesses going stale.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: several 2026 models failed to run reliably (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Pro, GLM-4.5 routing incompatibilities), which the paper calls harness staleness.

items.question: Does the paper show that models released in 2026 are more jailbreak-safe than 2024–25 models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper reports no such cohort comparison. Jailbreak safety spans most of the scale even among high-capability models, and release date is collinear with organization and capability, so any cohort difference would be observational and confounded.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: no release-cohort comparison is reported, and release date is entangled with organization and capability, so any difference would be confounded and observational.

items.question: Does a high XSTest safe-subset over-refusal rate show that a model will score high on R-Judge recall? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper only remarks that a model labelling too many traces as unsafe may score well on recall-oriented metrics. It reports no XSTest–R-Judge association. The tasks also differ (refusing prompts versus judging traces), and the XSTest comparisons have low power at n=17–20.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: no XSTest–R-Judge relationship is reported; the tasks differ and the XSTest comparison panel is small and low-power.

items.question: Does the passing of the paper's pre-specified harness controls show that each audited benchmark measures its intended target behavior? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The positive control checks that the two capability anchors agree, and the negative control checks that the pipeline does not create structure from noise. Neither tests any benchmark's target. The convergent control, the only one involving benchmark targets, was inconclusive at AgentDojo's n=5, and the blind coding shows only that the target labels can be recovered.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the positive and negative controls test pipeline behavior (anchor agreement, no structure from noise), not the benchmarks' targets.
Notes that the convergent control was inconclusive (n=5) and/or that the coding shows only recoverability.
